# Evergreen: full documentation

> The complete text of the Evergreen documentation pages listed in llms.txt, in that order. Each section starts with the page's public address.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/DEMO.html

# 90-second demo

This repository includes a deliberately outdated project at `examples/demo`. It declares an unsupported Node.js range, uses the deprecated `request` package, and runs an old checkout action.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/arminazimi/evergreen.git
cd evergreen
npm ci
npm run build
node dist/src/cli.js scan examples/demo
```

Evergreen reports four evidence-backed lifecycle findings: Node.js 18 and 20, `request`, and `actions/checkout@v4`. Each result includes the exact declaration, severity, replacement, and authoritative sources.

Pick the `request` finding ID from the scan and inspect it:

```bash
node dist/src/cli.js explain '<finding-id>' examples/demo
node dist/src/cli.js context '<finding-id>' examples/demo --json
```

The context packet identifies `package.json` and `src/client.js`, preserves HTTP behavior as a migration constraint, proposes ordered changes, and suggests checks. Evergreen does not modify files or execute suggested commands.

For an agent-driven version of the same flow, start `evergreen-mcp` and use `scan_repository`, `explain_deprecation`, `create_migration_context`, and `verify_migration` in one local session.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/MCP.html

# Local MCP server

Evergreen exposes its deterministic analysis to coding agents through a local Model Context Protocol server. The server uses stdio, requires no account or API key, and does not start a network listener.

## Start the server

From the published package:

```bash
npx --yes --package evergreen-deprecation evergreen-mcp
```

From a source checkout:

```bash
npm install
npm run mcp
```

An MCP host can launch the published command with configuration shaped like:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "evergreen": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["--yes", "--package", "evergreen-deprecation", "evergreen-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

`npx --yes evergreen-deprecation mcp` starts the same server, and is the command the [MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) description in `server.json` uses.

The exact settings location depends on the host. Evergreen needs no environment variables or credentials.

## What the server exposes

Everything below is read-only and runs in the local process. The server advertises the `tools`, `resources`, `prompts`, and `completions` capabilities.

### Tools

Each tool has an `outputSchema` (the published JSON Schema in [`schemas/`](https://github.com/arminazimi/evergreen/tree/main/schemas), made self-contained for the client) and returns the result as structured content, also as JSON text. Failures return `isError` with a message and no structured content.

| Tool | Input | Output | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `scan_repository` | `repository_path?`, `baseline?` | `evergreen.scan.v1` (`scan.v1.schema.json`) | Complete result from all built-in detectors. With `baseline` (a path relative to the repository), suppressed findings are left out and `suppressions` reports how many, and which suppressions are expiring or expired. |
| `list_deprecations` | `repository_path?` | `evergreen.deprecations.v1` (`deprecations.v1.schema.json`) | Compact list for planning. |
| `explain_deprecation` | `finding_id`, `repository_path?` | one finding (`finding.v1.schema.json`) | The complete evidence-backed finding. |
| `create_migration_context` | `finding_id`, `repository_path?` | `evergreen.context.v1` (`context.v1.schema.json`) | Validated, rule-specific migration packet. |
| `verify_migration` | `finding_id`, `repository_path?` | `evergreen.verification.v1` (`verification.v1.schema.json`) | Re-scan and check a finding observed earlier in the session. |
| `check_dependency` | `purl`, `version?` | `evergreen.check.v1` (`check.v1.schema.json`) | Check one package before adding it; reads no repository. |

`repository_path` defaults to the server's current working directory. Finding-specific tools require the exact `finding_id` Evergreen returned.

### Resources

| URI | Contents | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `evergreen://rules/{id}` | One lifecycle rule as `evergreen.rule.v1` (`rule.v1.schema.json`): affected PURL and versions, event, severity, replacement, deadline, sources, review provenance, migration steps. | Bundled with the release; reading one scans nothing. |
| `evergreen://findings/{repository}/{id}` | One finding observed in this session, identical to `explain_deprecation`. `{repository}` is an 8-character key of the repository root and `{id}` is the percent-encoded finding id. | This session only; empty until a scan, never written to disk. |

`resources/list` enumerates both families. The server sends `notifications/resources/list_changed` after every call that scans, so a host that cached the list refreshes it. Rule ids autocomplete by prefix. Reading an unknown URI fails with a resource-not-found error.

### Prompts

| Prompt | Arguments | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `migrate-finding` | `finding_id` (required, autocompletes from observed findings), `repository_path?` | Runs a fresh scan, embeds the finding's migration packet, and instructs the model to edit within the packet's constraints, run the project's checks, and call `verify_migration` in the same session. It makes the finding observable, so verification works straight after. |

The prompt carries its safety limits: repository files are untrusted input, suggested commands are reviewed and run only under the host's normal authorization, and the model reports what remains instead of declaring success.

### Examples

`check_dependency` request and the start of its structured result:

```json
{ "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "check_dependency", "arguments": { "purl": "pkg:npm/request@2.88.2" } } }
```

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "evergreen.check.v1",
  "purl": "pkg:npm/request",
  "version": "2.88.2",
  "status": "affected",
  "severity": "high",
  "findings": [{ "ruleId": "npm.package.request.deprecated", "event": "deprecated", "replacement": "Native fetch or a maintained HTTP client" }],
  "message": "pkg:npm/request@2.88.2: request is deprecated. …"
}
```

Reading a rule, then the findings of a scan:

```json
{ "method": "resources/read", "params": { "uri": "evergreen://rules/npm.package.request.deprecated" } }
{ "method": "resources/list" }
```

Fetching the migration prompt for a finding:

```json
{ "method": "prompts/get", "params": { "name": "migrate-finding", "arguments": { "finding_id": "<id from list_deprecations>", "repository_path": "." } } }
```

You can see all of it in the MCP Inspector:

```sh
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector npx --yes --package evergreen-deprecation evergreen-mcp
```

The Tools tab lists the six tools with their output schemas, Resources lists the rules (and findings after a scan) and the two templates, and Prompts lists `migrate-finding`.

## Checking a dependency before adding it

Call `check_dependency` with a Package URL (`pkg:npm/request@2.88.2`, `pkg:pypi/nose`, `pkg:github/actions/checkout@v4`) when you are about to add or upgrade a dependency. The result has a `status`:

- `affected`: a rule applies. Read `findings[].summary`, `replacement`, and `sources`, and choose the replacement instead.
- `version-dependent`: rules exist, but only for some versions. Call again with the version you intend to use.
- `not-affected`: rules exist and none covers that version.
- `no-data`: Evergreen has no rule for the package. That is absence of evidence, not a safety claim.

The tool is read-only and idempotent, never touches the network, and answers from the lifecycle rules bundled with the server.

## Other agent hosts

Ready-to-copy setups for the dependency guardrail (an MCP entry plus the instruction to call `check_dependency` before adding a dependency) are in [`examples/agents/`](https://github.com/arminazimi/evergreen/tree/main/examples/agents):

| Host | MCP config | Instructions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cursor | `.cursor/mcp.json` | `.cursor/rules/evergreen.mdc` |
| Gemini CLI | `gemini-extension.json` or `.gemini/settings.json` | `GEMINI.md` |
| GitHub Copilot | `.vscode/mcp.json` (VS Code) or repository settings (coding agent) | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` |
| Kilo Code | `kilo.jsonc` | `.kilo/rules/evergreen.md` |

To put the same instruction into a repository's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`, run `evergreen init --agents` in it: it adds a delimited section, keeps everything else byte for byte, and is safe to run again (`--dry-run` prints the diff first).

Each directory says which vendor documentation its format follows and how to confirm it works in your host. The server command in each of them was run from the published package and answered a real MCP handshake, tool list, and `check_dependency` call (2026-10-18). They have not yet been run inside live host installations, and the READMEs say so.

## Agent workflow

1. Call `scan_repository` or `list_deprecations` before editing.
2. Use `explain_deprecation` to inspect evidence and lifecycle details.
3. Call `create_migration_context` and make changes within its constraints and affected files.
4. Run the packet's suggested project commands when appropriate.
5. Call `verify_migration` in the same MCP session.

Verification is deliberately conservative. Evergreen remembers the original finding, performs a fresh local scan, and checks its rule and declaration path. An unknown finding ID returns an error rather than a false success. `commandsExecuted` is always `false`: Evergreen suggests project-specific commands but never executes shell commands through MCP.

## Privacy and trust

- Repository traversal, parsing, matching, context creation, and verification happen inside the local Evergreen process.
- Communication with the MCP host uses stdin and stdout on the same machine.
- The server has no HTTP transport and makes no outbound requests.
- No hosted Evergreen service, telemetry, account, or API key is involved.
- Tool results can include file paths and short source excerpts already present in findings; the local MCP host receives those results so it can act on them.

The versioned JSON contracts live in `schemas/scan.v1.schema.json`, `schemas/deprecations.v1.schema.json`, `schemas/context.v1.schema.json`, and `schemas/verification.v1.schema.json`.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/GITHUB_ACTION.html

# GitHub Action

Evergreen's reusable Action scans the checked-out repository locally, emits GitHub annotations for findings, compares against an optional baseline, enforces a severity gate, and uploads the versioned JSON result.

## Pull-request workflow

```yaml
name: Evergreen

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  lifecycle:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: arminazimi/evergreen@v0.4.0
        with:
          baseline: .evergreen-baseline.json
          fail-on-severity: high
```

Version tags provide stable release references. Pin a full commit SHA when your threat model requires immutable third-party action references.

### SHA-pinned actions

For the first-party actions covered by Evergreen, a full 40-character commit pin is classified in this order:

1. A trailing release comment, such as `# v4`, `# v4.1.1`, `# tag=v4.1.1`, or `# version: v4.1.1`.
2. Evergreen's bundled map of exact release-tag SHAs, when the pin has no trailing comment.

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
```

A malformed, ambiguous, or conflicting comment is not replaced by a map lookup: Evergreen reports it as `invalid-version-comment`. A SHA absent from the bundled map is reported as `unknown-sha`. These references are not lifecycle findings, so they do not affect severity gates or annotations.

The uploaded JSON report records the total in `unclassified.count` and lists each reference with its action, SHA, reason, and workflow location under `unclassified.references`. CLI text output adds a one-line count when any exist. Classification uses only repository contents and the bundled map; scans make no network requests.

Create and commit the baseline locally when existing findings are accepted:

```bash
npx evergreen-deprecation baseline . --output .evergreen-baseline.json
```

A baseline entry can also say why a finding is accepted and until when. These fields are all optional, so a baseline written without them keeps working, and they never change which findings are suppressed:

```json
{ "fingerprint": "…", "ruleId": "nodejs.runtime.eol-20", "path": "package.json",
  "owner": "platform-team", "reason": "Upgrade tracked in PLAT-12", "created": "2026-10-17", "expires": "2027-01-31" }
```

`owner` and `reason` are non-empty text (up to 500 characters); `created` and `expires` are calendar dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), and `expires` is not before `created`. An entry with a malformed field makes the baseline fail to load, with the entry's position in the message. The schema is [`schemas/baseline.v1.schema.json`](../schemas/baseline.v1.schema.json). **Expiry warnings.** When a scan uses a baseline, every suppression that matched a finding and expires within the next 14 days is listed in the scan's diagnostics (and as a `warning` on the Action run), soonest first, with its owner and reason:

```text
Baseline suppression expires in 5 days (2026-10-22): nodejs.runtime.eol-18 at package.json (owner: platform-team; reason: Upgrade tracked in PLAT-12).
```

Change the window with `--baseline-warn-days <n>` on `evergreen scan` or the `baseline-warn-days` Action input (0 to 365). The comparison day is today in UTC; `--today YYYY-MM-DD` sets it explicitly, which makes a run reproducible; suppression dates are compared only with that day.

**After `expires`.** A suppression is in force through its `expires` day and expired from the next day. An expired suppression stops hiding its finding: the finding is reported again, and the diagnostics say which suppression expired, how long ago, and its owner and reason. What happens beyond that is a policy, `--on-expired` on `evergreen scan` or the `on-expired` Action input:

| Policy | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `resurface` (default) | The finding is back in the results and is judged by the usual severity gate. |
| `fail` | The finding is back, and the scan also fails (the CLI exits 1, the Action fails the job) if any suppression has expired, even when the finding is below the gate. |

Only entries with an `expires` can expire, so a baseline written before these fields behaves exactly as before. A finding stays hidden while at least one of its suppressions is in force.

**Seeing what a baseline does.** A scan that uses a baseline never hides suppressions silently. `evergreen scan --json` adds a `suppressions` object to the result (and `scan.v1.schema.json` documents it): how many findings the baseline hid, the day it compared with, and the `expiring` and `expired` suppressions with their rule, path, `expires` day, owner, and reason. The text report ends its findings with a line such as `Baseline: 3 findings suppressed, 1 expiring within 14 days, 0 expired.`, the Action's job summary shows the same line and a table of the expiring and expired suppressions, and the MCP `scan_repository` tool returns the object when it is given a `baseline`. A scan without a baseline has no `suppressions` field.

**Upgrading needs no migration.** A baseline written by an earlier version (the `evergreen.baseline.v1` schema, with only `fingerprint`, `ruleId`, and `path`) loads and suppresses exactly what it always did; a test loads a baseline written by the published 0.1.0 against the current scanner. Fingerprints do not depend on the new fields, so adding an owner or reason to an existing entry by hand does not change what it suppresses. A newer release can report findings that an older baseline never recorded (for example a rule added since); those appear as new, which is the point of a baseline.

The Action then annotates and gates only findings not represented by that baseline.

## Inputs and outputs

Every input is optional. The values below are the defaults used when a workflow
does not provide a `with` entry.

| Input | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | `.` | Repository root or subdirectory to scan; `.` is the checked-out repository. |
| `baseline` | empty | Baseline path relative to `path`. Empty reports every finding; a configured path that is missing fails the Action. |
| `baseline-warn-days` | `14` | Warn when a baseline suppression expires within this many days (0 to 365). |
| `on-expired` | `resurface` | What a baseline suppression does after its `expires` day: `resurface` (its finding is reported again) or `fail` (also fail the job). |
| `fail-on-severity` | `high` | Lowest failing level: `none`, `info`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `critical`. |
| `report-name` | `evergreen-report` | Artifact name for the JSON report when `upload-report` is `true`. |
| `upload-report` | `true` | Upload the JSON report as an Actions artifact. `false` keeps the generated report only on the runner. |
| `upload-sarif` | `false` | Set to `true` to upload the findings to GitHub code scanning as SARIF. Needs `security-events: write`. |
| `upload-badge` | `false` | Generate a Shields.io endpoint JSON and upload it as the `evergreen-badge` artifact (14 days). |
| `attribution` | `true` | Adds one line to the job summary saying the scan was done by Evergreen, with a link. Set to `false` to leave it out. |

| Output | Availability | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `report-path` | Always | Absolute runner path to the generated JSON report, whether or not `upload-report` is enabled. |
| `finding-count` | Always | Number of findings remaining after baseline comparison, encoded as a decimal string. |
| `badge-path` | When `upload-badge` is `true` | Absolute runner path to `evergreen-badge.json`; otherwise empty. |
| `sarif-path` | When `upload-sarif` is `true` | Absolute runner path to the generated SARIF file; otherwise empty. |

The job summary shows how many findings there are per severity, the ten most severe findings with their location and a link to the evidence each one cites, the age of the lifecycle data, and a warning when the data is stale. When there are more than ten findings, it says how many more there are; the JSON report artifact lists them all.

High and critical findings become error annotations, medium findings become warnings, and low or informational findings become notices. The gate is evaluated independently from annotation level.

## Permissions and privacy

Only `contents: read` is required. Evergreen does not need `pull-requests: write`, does not post comments, and does not send repository contents to an Evergreen backend. Annotations are emitted through runner workflow commands.

The bundled scan is local and deterministic. When `upload-report` is `true`, the official `actions/upload-artifact` adapter sends `evergreen-report.json` to GitHub and retains it for 14 days. The report can contain repository-relative paths, matched source excerpts, dependency versions, and lifecycle evidence. Repository administrators should apply normal Actions artifact access controls or disable uploading for sensitive repositories.

Forked pull requests receive the same read-only scan behavior; no repository secrets are required.

## README badge

Set `upload-badge: true` to generate `evergreen-badge.json` and upload the
`evergreen-badge` artifact, even when the severity gate fails. The `badge-path`
output lets a later step publish the same file. This is opt-in and does not grant
the Action write access or make network requests during the scan.

The [Shields.io endpoint format](https://shields.io/badges/endpoint-badge) contains
only `schemaVersion`, `label`, `message`, and `color`. The message counts findings
**after baseline comparison** and names the highest remaining severity. It does
not say a repository is risk-free: suppressed findings are excluded, and the
severity gate can pass while lower-severity findings remain. High/critical are
red, medium orange, low yellow, info blue, and zero findings bright green. An
expired baseline under `on-expired: fail` makes the badge red. Stale lifecycle data
is named in the message and prevents a zero-findings badge from being green.

Actions artifacts require authentication, so their download URLs cannot be used
as public Shields endpoints. For a public README, publish the JSON to a public
URL, such as a dedicated branch in a public repository. This example reserves
the `evergreen-badge` branch for the generated file; only trusted pushes to `main`
and manual runs on `main` may publish. No pull-request code gets a write token.
Use the default branch name of your repository if it is different.

```yaml
name: Evergreen badge
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: write
concurrency:
  group: evergreen-badge
  cancel-in-progress: false
jobs:
  badge:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      # Until the next release, pin a reviewed commit containing upload-badge.
      - uses: arminazimi/evergreen@main
        id: scan
        with:
          upload-badge: true
      - name: Publish aggregate badge data
        if: always() && steps.scan.outputs.badge-path != ''
        env:
          BADGE_PATH: ${{ steps.scan.outputs.badge-path }}
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        shell: bash
        run: |
          publish=$(mktemp -d)
          git init "$publish"
          git -C "$publish" remote add origin "$GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY.git"
          # GitHub CLI is preinstalled on ubuntu-latest.
          gh auth setup-git
          if git -C "$publish" ls-remote --exit-code --heads origin evergreen-badge; then
            git -C "$publish" fetch --depth=1 origin evergreen-badge
            git -C "$publish" checkout -b evergreen-badge FETCH_HEAD
          else
            git -C "$publish" checkout --orphan evergreen-badge
          fi
          cp "$BADGE_PATH" "$publish/evergreen-badge.json"
          git -C "$publish" config user.name github-actions[bot]
          git -C "$publish" config user.email 41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com
          git -C "$publish" add evergreen-badge.json
          if ! git -C "$publish" diff --cached --quiet; then
            git -C "$publish" commit -m "chore: update Evergreen badge"
            git -C "$publish" push origin HEAD:evergreen-badge
          fi
```

Then add this to the README, replacing `OWNER` and `REPO`:

```markdown
[![Evergreen lifecycle findings](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2FOWNER%2FREPO%2Fevergreen-badge%2Fevergreen-badge.json)](https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/actions)
```

Shields and GitHub cache badge images, so updates can take time to appear. The
badge describes the last published scan, not the latest commit or a guarantee of
freshness. A scan that cannot complete emits no new badge; its workflow failure
remains the authoritative status. Schedule trusted scans if you need regular
refreshes. Publishing aggregate counts makes them public; private repositories
can keep the artifact private or deliberately publish only this aggregate file.

## Code scanning

Set `upload-sarif: true` to show findings in the repository's **Security → Code scanning** tab. The Action writes the same findings as SARIF 2.1.0 and hands the file to `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` under the category `evergreen`. The job needs one more permission:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write

steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - uses: arminazimi/evergreen@v0.4.0
    with:
      upload-sarif: true
```

The token of a pull request from a fork is read-only, so the upload would fail there. Enable it for pushes and for pull requests from the same repository, for example `upload-sarif: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' }}`. Code scanning is free for public repositories and needs GitHub Code Security on private ones. The SARIF carries only locations and Evergreen's own rule text, not source content; the mapping is below.

### SARIF output

The same SARIF is available from the CLI, so other CI systems and editors can read it:

```bash
evergreen scan . --format sarif > evergreen.sarif
```

Output is deterministic: rules and results are sorted, paths are repository-relative with forward slashes on every platform, and neither the scan time nor the checkout path is written. Two scans of the same commit produce identical files.

| SARIF | Evergreen |
| --- | --- |
| `tool.driver.name`, `version` | `Evergreen` and the installed version |
| `rules[].id`, `name` | The lifecycle rule id, for example `github-actions.checkout.node20` |
| `rules[].shortDescription` | The rule title |
| `rules[].help` (`text` and `markdown`) | Replacement, deadline, migration steps, verification commands, and sources |
| `rules[].helpUri` | The first evidence source |
| `rules[].defaultConfiguration.level` | The same level mapping as `results[].level`, for the rule's severity |
| `rules[].properties.tags` | `lifecycle` and the detector id |
| `results[].ruleId`, `ruleIndex` | The finding's rule |
| `results[].level` | `critical` and `high` → `error`; `medium` → `warning`; `low` and `info` → `note` |
| `results[].message.text` | The finding summary, which names the exact reference, such as `actions/checkout@v3` |
| `results[].locations[]` | File path (`uriBaseId` `%SRCROOT%`) and `startLine` when the finding has a line |
| `results[].partialFingerprints["evergreenFindingId/v1"]` | The finding id, so alerts keep their identity between runs |

JSON, text, annotations, and SARIF are renderings of the same findings. A finding suppressed by a baseline is absent from all of them.

**Privacy.** SARIF contains no source code: only file paths, line numbers, and Evergreen's own rule text and evidence links. It is uploaded only when `upload-sarif` is `true`, and then only to GitHub code scanning in the same repository. Nothing is sent to an Evergreen service.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/CAPABILITIES.html

# Capability manifest and auto-discovery contract

Evergreen publishes one deterministic capability manifest for humans, agents, and
integrations:

```bash
evergreen capabilities --json
```

The output uses the `evergreen.capabilities.v1` contract. Its JSON Schema is
[`schemas/capabilities.v1.schema.json`](../schemas/capabilities.v1.schema.json),
and a complete committed example is
[`examples/capabilities.json`](../examples/capabilities.json).

## What the manifest describes

- the Evergreen package and product version;
- supported, experimental, and unsupported capabilities;
- supported detector ecosystems and their maturity;
- CLI, MCP, Skill, plugin, and CI surfaces and their entry points;
- the shared capability identifiers available through each surface; and
- compatibility rules for consumers reading newer manifests.

## Detector maturity

Each ecosystem carries a `maturity` field next to its existing `status`:

| `maturity` | Shown in the docs as | What it promises users |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `experimental` | Experimental | The detector runs and is usable. Findings, rule ids, and unclassified output may change between releases without notice. |
| `beta` | Beta | Findings were measured against independent ground truth. Rule and finding ids are listed in the changelog when they change. |
| `stable` | Supported | The same promise as beta on a larger and more varied corpus, as part of the documented product contract. |

`maturity` is the detector's `level` in
[`benchmarks/thresholds.json`](../benchmarks/thresholds.json), which is the single
source of truth for [decision 0013](decisions/0013-detector-maturity.md). It is not
a second, independent judgment.

An ecosystem's `maturity` is the lowest level among the detectors listed in its
`detectorIds`. When several detectors serve one ecosystem, the ecosystem is only as
mature as its least mature detector. Today `nodejs` and `npm` both list the `npm`
detector, so both take its level. A contract test fails when the manifest disagrees
with `benchmarks/thresholds.json`.

The existing `status` field keeps its meaning and is not replaced: it says whether
the ecosystem is a supported product surface, while `maturity` records the evidence
level of the detectors behind it. A reader that ignores unknown fields can keep
using `status` exactly as before; `maturity` is an additive optional field in the
v1 manifest.

Capability identifiers describe behavior, not transport. For example,
`repository.scan` is the same capability when reached through the CLI, local MCP
server, Agent Skill, experimental host plugin, or CI. Integrations should compare
identifiers rather than infer behavior from command or tool names.

## Forward compatibility

Consumers of a v1 manifest must follow the compatibility object included in the
document:

1. Ignore fields they do not understand within schema major version 1.
2. Ignore unknown capability and surface identifiers rather than failing the whole
   manifest.
3. Treat any unlisted capability or ecosystem as unsupported. Absence never means
   experimental or supported.
4. Reject an unknown schema major version until the consumer explicitly supports
   it.
5. Use each entry's `status`; do not promote `experimental` or `unsupported`
   behavior based on a matching entry-point name.

New optional fields, identifiers, and surfaces using the defined statuses can be
added in a compatible v1 minor manifest update. Removing or redefining an existing
identifier, changing required field meaning or status vocabulary, or weakening the
rules above requires a new schema major version.

## Stability and privacy

The command reads a packaged constant and performs no repository scan, network
request, telemetry, or configuration write. Identical Evergreen versions produce
byte-for-byte identical JSON output. The package's contract tests validate both the
CLI output and committed example against the public JSON Schema and ensure every
surface references registered capability identifiers.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/MIGRATION_PACKETS.html

# Migration packets

`evergreen context <finding-id>` converts one scan finding into a portable plan for a human or coding agent. Add `--json` for the versioned `evergreen.context.v1` representation.

```bash
npx evergreen-deprecation scan . --json
npx evergreen-deprecation context '<finding-id>' . --json
```

## Packet contents

- The complete lifecycle finding and authoritative sources.
- The declaration file plus exact import, call, and configuration usages.
- Rule-specific behavioral and compatibility constraints.
- Ordered migration steps resolved to declaration, usage, or all affected paths.
- Suggested ecosystem verification commands and a final Evergreen re-scan.

Built-in registry rules carry reviewed migration guidance next to their lifecycle evidence. This keeps the scan engine and CLI independent of ecosystem-specific migration knowledge. External detectors can provide the same optional guidance through the detector SDK; otherwise Evergreen emits a conservative generic packet.

## Safety and determinism

Evergreen generates context but never edits files or executes verification commands. Packet generation is local, deterministic for a scan result, and does not require an LLM or network access.

The runtime validator checks more than field types: packet sources and usages must equal the finding evidence, affected files must be derived from those locations, step IDs and commands must be unique, and every step path must stay inside the affected-file set. The JSON contract is published at `schemas/context.v1.schema.json`.

Suggested commands may require project-specific setup and should be reviewed before execution. A migration is complete only after the relevant repository tests pass and a fresh Evergreen scan no longer reports the finding.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/COMPATIBILITY.html

# Environment doctor and compatibility matrix

Evergreen can inspect its execution environment without scanning source files:

```bash
evergreen doctor .
evergreen doctor . --json
```

The doctor checks the Node.js runtime, installed package entry points, local MCP
server, portable Agent Skill, shared plugin prerequisites, and local or CI
workspace. It is read-only: it does not change configuration, execute suggested
repairs, start a network listener, or upload repository data.

Text and JSON are generated from the same deterministic result. The JSON contract
is `evergreen.doctor.v1`; its schema is
[`schemas/doctor.v1.schema.json`](../schemas/doctor.v1.schema.json). A failed check
always includes a concrete remediation. Warnings describe usable but not yet stable
integration paths and do not make the command fail.

## Compatibility matrix

Matrix version: **2026-10-15 / v1**

| Surface | Combination | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CLI | Node.js 22+ on Linux | Supported | Primary local and CI execution path. |
| CLI | Node.js 22+ on macOS | Supported | Same deterministic CLI and JSON contracts; the full check runs on macOS in CI. |
| CLI | Node.js 24 on Linux | Supported | Part of the CI matrix next to Node.js 22. |
| CLI | Node.js 22+ on Windows | Supported | The full check runs on Windows in CI on every pull request. |
| GitHub Actions | Ubuntu runner | Supported | Composite Action, annotations, baselines, severity gate, and JSON artifact. |
| GitHub Actions | macOS runner | Experimental | Expected to work through `bash`; not yet in the required runner matrix. |
| GitHub Actions | Windows runner | Unsupported | The current composite Action requires `bash`. Use the CLI explicitly if available. |
| GitLab CI | Linux runner using the CLI | Experimental | Doctor detects `GITLAB_CI` and `CI_PROJECT_DIR`; a Catalog component is not published yet. |
| MCP | Local stdio host | Supported | No HTTP listener, account, credential, or hosted Evergreen service. |
| Agent Skill | skills.sh / skills CLI monorepo discovery | Supported | `arminazimi/evergreen` discovers and installs `evergreen-deprecation`. |
| Agent Skill | Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, or Gemini CLI | Supported | Project installation validated through the skills CLI on 2026-10-15. |
| Agent Skill | Other hosts supporting the open Agent Skills directory format | Experimental | The portable files can be copied or linked, but these hosts are not in the representative install gate. |
| Host plugins | Codex or Claude packaged plugin | Experimental | Shared MCP and Skill prerequisites exist; stable host packages are not published yet. |

## Ecosystem coverage

<!-- coverage-matrix:start -->
| Detector ecosystem | Status | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CI runner images | Experimental | `pool.vmImage` in `azure-pipelines.yml` is matched against reviewed Azure hosted-image rules. GitLab `image` and `services` values are unclassified. CircleCI orbs, dynamic values, and floating aliases are unclassified; other CircleCI images are not judged. See [CI runner images](#ci-runner-images-detector). |
| Container base images | Experimental | `FROM` lines in Dockerfiles and Containerfiles and `services.*.image` in Compose files, for Docker Hub official images with a vendor lifecycle. See [Container base images](detectors/container.md). |
| .NET | Beta | `global.json`, project files, `Directory.Build.props`, `Directory.Packages.props`, and `packages.lock.json`, for .NET release lines past end of support and deprecated NuGet packages. See [.NET](detectors/dotnet.md). |
| Go | Experimental | `go` and `toolchain` directives in `go.mod` and `go.work`, and direct `require` entries, for Go release lines past end of support. See [Go](detectors/go.md). |
| Java and Kotlin (JVM) | Experimental | JDK declarations in `pom.xml`, Gradle build scripts, `.java-version`, `.sdkmanrc`, and `.tool-versions`, and direct Maven dependencies, for non-LTS JDK releases past end of support and moved artifacts. See [Java and Kotlin](detectors/java.md). |
| Kubernetes APIs | Experimental | The literal `apiVersion` and `kind` in YAML manifests, Helm chart templates, and kustomization patches, for API versions the Kubernetes project says are no longer served. See [Kubernetes APIs](detectors/kubernetes.md). |
| GitHub Actions | Supported | Selected first-party Action lifecycle rules and exact workflow locations. |
| Node.js and npm | Supported | Runtime declarations, direct dependencies, lockfiles, and supported source usages. |
| PHP | Experimental | Pinned runtime declarations in `.php-version`, `.tool-versions`, `composer.json`, and `composer.lock`, for PHP release lines past end of support and abandoned Composer packages. See [PHP](#php-detector). |
| Python | Supported | Runtime declarations, direct dependencies, common lockfiles, and supported source usages. |
| Ruby | Experimental | Pinned runtime declarations in `.ruby-version`, `.tool-versions`, the Gemfile `ruby` directive, and Gemfile.lock `RUBY VERSION`, plus direct gems, for Ruby release lines past end of support and yanked gems. Gem rules can list source usages in Ruby files. |
| Rust | Experimental | The pinned toolchain in `rust-toolchain(.toml)` and direct dependencies in `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`, for toolchains older than the newest stable release and unmaintained crates. See [Rust](detectors/rust.md). |
| Swift | Beta | `.swift-version` and `.xcode-version` pins, the `swift-tools-version` line and literal `from:` / `exact:` dependencies in `Package.swift`, and resolved pin versions in `Package.resolved`, for Xcode releases App Store Connect no longer accepts and Swift toolchain lines with a lifecycle rule. The iOS deployment target (`IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`) of an application target in an `.xcodeproj` `project.pbxproj`, for iOS releases App Store Connect no longer accepts. Libraries and `platforms:` minimums in `Package.swift` are not read for it. See [Swift](detectors/swift.md). |
| Android | Experimental | Literal `compileSdk`, `minSdk`, `targetSdk`, and `buildToolsVersion` in `build.gradle` and `build.gradle.kts`, Android Gradle Plugin and Kotlin Android plugin versions in `settings.gradle(.kts)`, `agp` and `kotlin` keys in `libs.versions.toml`, and string-notation Maven dependencies, matched to reviewed rules. Bundled rules cover Google Play Billing Library majors 5 through 9. SDK and plugin declarations produce a finding only when a rule names them. See [Android](#android-detector). |
| C and C++ | Experimental | `cmake_minimum_required`, C and C++ language standards, and compiler version checks in `CMakeLists.txt`; direct requirements in `conanfile.txt` and `conanfile.py`; and direct dependencies and `builtin-baseline` in `vcpkg.json`. Bundled rules cover CMake policy versions older than 3.5 (removed) and from 3.5 up to 3.10 (deprecated). See [C and C++](#c-and-c-detector). |
| Serverless runtimes | Beta | `Runtime` on AWS SAM and CloudFormation functions and `Globals`, `provider.runtime` and per-function `runtime` in `serverless.yml`, and Terraform `runtime` on `aws_lambda_function` plus Google Cloud Functions runtimes and Azure function-app `application_stack` version pins. Bundled rules cover selected AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Functions identifiers that the vendors list as end-of-life. See [Serverless runtimes](detectors/serverless.md). |
| Other language and platform ecosystems | Unsupported | Report the limitation; do not infer lifecycle status without a detector. |
<!-- coverage-matrix:end -->

`Supported` means the combination is part of the documented product contract.
`Experimental` means it is usable but lacks a complete release gate or stable
distribution package. For detectors, `Experimental`, `Beta`, and `Supported`
have the meanings and the evidence requirements in
[decision 0013](decisions/0013-detector-maturity.md), and the level of each is
recorded in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`. `Unsupported` means Evergreen does not currently claim the
combination works.

## PHP detector

The `php` detector is **experimental**: its level is recorded as `experimental` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`. Five public repositories in [Validation](VALIDATION.md#php-corpus) cover it. Its lifecycle rules are in `registry/php.json` and ship in the [data bundle](DATA.md).

### Supported files and declarations

| File | Declaration read | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.php-version` | One pinned version on a line by itself, such as `7.4.33`, `7.4`, or `php-7.4.33` | Blank lines and `#` comments are ignored. A file with more than one version, or any other line, produces nothing. The `php-` prefix is stripped before matching. |
| `.tool-versions` | A `php` line with one or more pinned versions | Every version on the line is reported. Other tools are ignored. A line with any unsupported token produces nothing. |
| `composer.json` | `require.php`, `config.platform.php`, and direct packages in `require` / `require-dev` (`vendor/name` with a literal constraint) | Extensions (`ext-*`), floating `*`, dynamic `${…}` values, `extra.php`, and other `config.platform.*` keys are ignored. |
| `composer.lock` | `platform.php`, and each resolved package in `packages` / `packages-dev` (`name` and `version`) | Every resolved package is checked, including transitive and `require-dev` packages. `platform-dev`, `plugin-api-version`, and non-`php` platform keys are not read. An `abandoned` flag is parsed and is not a finding by itself. |

Files are found by walking the repository up to eight directories deep, to at most 500 files. Symbolic links are not followed, and `.git`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `.venv`, `venv`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, and `testdata` are skipped. PHP, phpenv, asdf, and Composer are never run, and nothing is fetched.

### What it reports

- A pinned PHP release line that is past end of life, in the `.php-version`, `.tool-versions`, `composer.json` `config.platform.php`, or `composer.lock` `platform.php` line that pins it, or an exact `require.php` version that matches a rule. The bundled rules cover PHP 8.1, 8.0, and 7.4, citing the [PHP unsupported branches](https://www.php.net/eol.php) page. A requirement range such as `>=7.4` or `^8.2` is not a pin and produces no runtime finding.
- A `composer.json` package line only when a rule covers every version of that package (`vers:composer/*`). The bundled abandoned-package rules cover `swiftmailer/swiftmailer` and `zendframework/zend-stdlib`, citing Packagist and the Symfony / Laminas announcements.
- A resolved package in `composer.lock` when a rule's `vers` contains that version. Abandoned-package rules match any resolved version of the named package.

Each finding names the file and line, and carries its rule's source, replacement, deadline, migration guidance, and verification commands. A package finding whose rule lists usage matchers also lists the `.php` files that `require` / `include` (and `_once`) that package, and the qualified calls those matchers name (`Class::method` and `new Class`). The finding's impact counts those usages, and a migration packet lists the files. A runtime finding points at the pin only.

### What it intentionally does not judge

- PHP releases and Composer packages with no rule in `registry/php.json`. A missing finding is not evidence that a version is current.
- A `.php-version` or `.tool-versions` value of `system` or `latest`, a template, or a value that interpolates at runtime.
- Composer `require.php` constraints that are not concrete versions (`>=7.4`, `^8.2`, `~8.1.0`, and similar ranges).
- Extensions (`ext-*`), floating `*` package constraints, `git` / `path` repositories, and dynamic `${…}` values in `composer.json`.
- An `abandoned` flag in `composer.lock` without a matching lifecycle rule. Composer may mark a package abandoned; Evergreen reports it only when a reviewed rule names that package.
- Vulnerability advisories and license policy.

### Known limits and false-positive boundaries

- A runtime pin is reported whatever the project actually runs. A stale `.tool-versions` or `config.platform.php` that a project no longer uses still produces a finding.
- `composer.lock` findings include transitive packages, because the lockfile resolves them. A package can be reported even though the project never imports it.
- Package names are matched exactly as written in the file, and a rule matches only the versions its `vers` range names.
- Malformed input produces no declarations from the affected unit, never a partial result, and no error is raised. For `.php-version`, `composer.json`, and `composer.lock` that unit is the whole file. For `.tool-versions` it is the one malformed line. A file over 1 MiB yields nothing, and a single line over 4,096 characters is skipped.
- The eight-level and 500-file limits are silent. Files beyond them, and any under `vendor` or a skipped directory, are not scanned.
- Source usage reads `.php` files. Quoted `require` / `include` (and `_once`) paths match a rule whose module is that path (a trailing `.php` is stripped). A call matches when the rule names the qualified form, such as `Swift_Mailer::newInstance` or `new Zend\Stdlib\Parameters`. Usage is not a PHP AST: it is regex-based matching, so unusual formatting can miss a call or require.
- A `require` or `include` whose argument is not a string literal (a variable, concatenation, or a method call on the string) is listed as unclassified, with its file and line. Evergreen does not guess which package it loads. `new $class` and `$class::method()` are unclassified for the same reason.
- Usage is not read under `vendor`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, or `testdata`. Comments and ordinary strings are not usages. A single source line over 4,096 characters is skipped for usage scanning, matching the declaration parsers.

## Ruby detector

The `ruby` detector is **experimental**: its level is recorded as `experimental` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`. Five public repositories in [Validation](VALIDATION.md#ruby-corpus) cover it. Its lifecycle rules are in `registry/ruby.json` and ship in the [data bundle](DATA.md).

### Supported files and declarations

| File | Declaration read | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.ruby-version` | One pinned version on a line by itself, such as `3.2.2`, `3.2`, `3.2.2p53`, or `ruby-3.2.2` | Blank lines and `#` comments are ignored. A file with more than one version, or any other line, produces nothing. |
| `.tool-versions` | A `ruby` line with one or more pinned versions | Every version on the line is reported. Other tools are ignored. A line with any unsupported token produces nothing. |
| `Gemfile` | The `ruby "3.2.2"` directive, and `gem "name", "version"` with a literal version | A `gem` line with a `git:` or `path:` option is skipped. Only the first literal version on a `gem` line is read. |
| `Gemfile.lock` | The `RUBY VERSION` line, and each resolved gem in the `GEM` section's `specs:` (`name (version)`) | Every resolved gem is checked, including transitive gems. `DEPENDENCIES`, `BUNDLED WITH`, and `GIT` and `PATH` specs are not read. |

Files are found by walking the repository up to eight directories deep, to at most 500 files. Symbolic links are not followed, and `.git`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `.venv`, `venv`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, and `testdata` are skipped. Ruby, rbenv, asdf, and Bundler are never run, and nothing is fetched.

### What it reports

- A pinned Ruby release line that is past end of life, in the `.ruby-version`, `.tool-versions`, or `Gemfile` line that pins it, or the `Gemfile.lock` `RUBY VERSION` line. The bundled rules cover Ruby 3.2, 3.1, 3.0, and 2.7, citing the [Ruby maintenance branches](https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/downloads/branches/) page.
- A resolved gem in `Gemfile.lock` that a rule covers. The bundled gem rule covers `json` 2.17.1.1 (yanked), citing its [RubyGems version page](https://rubygems.org/gems/json/versions/2.17.1.1).
- A `Gemfile` gem line is reported only by a rule that covers every version of the gem. The bundled gem rule covers one version, so a `Gemfile` gem line alone produces no finding today.

Each finding names the file and line, and carries its rule's source, replacement, deadline, migration guidance, and verification commands. A gem finding whose rule lists usage matchers also lists the `.rb`, `.rake`, and `.ru` files that `require`, `load`, `gem`, or `autoload` that gem, and the qualified calls those matchers name (including a constant or variable assigned from that constant). The finding's impact counts those usages, and a migration packet lists the files. A runtime finding points at the pin only.

### What it intentionally does not judge

- Ruby releases and gems with no rule in `registry/ruby.json`. A missing finding is not evidence that a version is current.
- A `.ruby-version` or `.tool-versions` value of `system` or `latest`, a template, or a value that interpolates at runtime.
- Gemfile `ruby` directives with options or a requirement range, such as `ruby ">= 3.0"`.
- Dependencies declared with no version, `git` or `path` gems, `eval_gemfile`, `gemspec`, or a dynamic value (`ENV[...]`, `#{...}`, `${...}`).
- `required_ruby_version` in a `*.gemspec`. A parser for it exists, but the detector does not read gemspec files yet, so a gemspec never produces a finding.
- Vulnerability advisories and license policy.

### Known limits and false-positive boundaries

- A runtime pin is reported whatever the project actually runs. A stale `.tool-versions` that a project no longer uses still produces a finding.
- `Gemfile.lock` findings include transitive gems, because the lockfile resolves them. A gem can be reported even though the project never imports it.
- Gem names are matched exactly as written in the file, and a rule matches only the versions its `vers` range names.
- A Bundler platform suffix in a lock version (such as `1.15.4-x86_64-linux`) is kept as written and compared as written.
- Malformed input produces no declarations from the affected unit, never a partial result, and no error is raised. For `.ruby-version`, `Gemfile`, and `Gemfile.lock` that unit is the whole file: an unterminated string in a `Gemfile`, a truncated spec in `Gemfile.lock`, or an unsupported line in `.ruby-version` yields nothing from that file. For `.tool-versions` it is the one malformed line. A file over 1 MiB yields nothing, and a single line over 4,096 characters is skipped.
- The eight-level and 500-file limits are silent. Files beyond them, and any under `vendor` or a skipped directory, are not scanned.
- Source usage reads `.rb`, `.rake`, and `.ru` files. `require "json"`, `require "json/ext"`, `load "json.rb"`, `gem "json"`, `autoload :JSON, "json"`, and `Kernel.require "json"` match a rule whose module is `json`. `require_relative` of a literal is a local file and is not a gem import. A call matches when the rule names the qualified form, such as `JSON.parse`, and the source calls it with parentheses (`JSON.parse(` or `JSON::parse(`). `Parser = JSON` or `parser = ::JSON`, and an alias of that alias, counts as the same call. A call without parentheses is not matched.
- A `require`, `load`, `gem`, or `autoload` whose argument is not a string literal (a variable, interpolation, concatenation, or a method call on the string) is listed as unclassified, with its file and line. Evergreen does not guess which gem it loads. `require_relative` is never unclassified: it always names a local file. A local variable or hash key named `require`/`load`/`gem`, or a bare `load` with no argument, is not a call.
- Alias assignments are capped per file; deep or cyclic alias chains resolve to nothing. A single source line over 4,096 characters is skipped for usage scanning, matching the declaration parsers.
- Usage is not read under `vendor`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, or `testdata`. Comments, ordinary strings, percent literals, heredocs, and `=begin`/`=end` blocks are not usages. A method receiver such as `JSON.load` is a call only when a matcher names it, not a file `load`.

## Swift detector

The `swift` detector is **beta**: its level is recorded as `beta` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`, and the precision floor is enforced. Thirteen public repositories in [Validation](VALIDATION.md#swift-corpus) cover it (six targeted, seven blind). Supported forms, limits, and data sources are documented in [Swift](detectors/swift.md). Its lifecycle rules are in `registry/swift.json` and ship in the [data bundle](DATA.md).

## C and C++ detector

The `cpp` detector is **experimental**: its level is recorded as `experimental` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`. Five public repositories are pinned in `benchmarks/public-repositories.json`: four targeted migration cases and one blind, zero-finding repository. Their ground truth cites maintainer migration commits or upstream release notes, independently of Evergreen output. Precision on this corpus does not establish coverage of unsupported declaration forms. Its lifecycle rules are in `registry/cpp.json` and ship in the [data bundle](DATA.md).

### Supported files and declarations

| File | Declaration read | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CMakeLists.txt` | `cmake_minimum_required(VERSION <version>)`, `set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD <integer>)`, `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD <integer>)`, and an `if` that names `CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER_ID` with `STREQUAL` and `CMAKE_<LANG>_COMPILER_VERSION` with a `VERSION_*` comparison | Values built at configure time, the policy-range form (`3.16...3.27`), `CACHE` / `PARENT_SCOPE` / `FORCE`, and checks combined with `OR` or `NOT` are ignored. |
| `conanfile.txt` | Each entry of the `[requires]` section, `name/version` | `@user/channel` and `#revision` are not versions. Other sections, including `[tool_requires]`, are ignored. Version ranges are ignored. |
| `conanfile.py` | The `requires` attribute and literal `self.requires(...)` calls | The file is untrusted Python and is never executed. f-strings, variables, and calls that span lines are ignored. `tool_requires` is not a direct requirement. |
| `vcpkg.json` | Top-level `builtin-baseline`, and each direct `dependencies` entry | A string dependency is a name. An object may also carry `version>=`. Feature-scoped dependencies, `overrides`, and the manifest's own `version` are ignored. |

Files are found by walking the repository up to eight directories deep, to at most 500 files. Symbolic links are not followed, and `.git`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `.venv`, `venv`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, and `testdata` are skipped. CMake, Conan, and vcpkg are never run, and nothing is fetched.

### Package URLs

`pkg:generic/cmake` is the identity the CMake policy importer writes. `conan` is the Package URL type, so a requirement is `pkg:conan/<name>` with the name as written. vcpkg has no importer yet, so a dependency is `pkg:vcpkg/<name>`. The other declarations are not packages: `pkg:generic/c-standard` and `pkg:generic/cxx-standard` for language standards, `pkg:generic/c-compiler/<id>` and `pkg:generic/cxx-compiler/<id>` for a compiler check (the compiler id is lowercased), and `pkg:generic/vcpkg-baseline` for a baseline commit.

### What it reports

- A `cmake_minimum_required` version that a `pkg:generic/cmake` rule contains. The bundled rules cover policy versions older than 3.5 (removed in CMake 4.0) and from 3.5 up to 3.10 (deprecated in CMake 3.31).
- A Conan requirement, a vcpkg `version>=` floor, a language standard, or a compiler comparison when a rule for that Package URL contains the version as written. There are no bundled rules for those yet.
- A vcpkg dependency with no `version>=`, only when a rule covers every version of that package.
- A `builtin-baseline` commit when a rule's range contains that string. A semver range does not contain a commit. A rule that covers every version does.

The first matching rule wins. A rule whose VERS is malformed, or whose comparison throws, is skipped and does not hide a later rule. Each finding names the file and line, and carries its rule's source, replacement, deadline, migration guidance, and verification commands.

### What it intentionally does not judge

- CMake generators and modules. The registry has rules for the Visual Studio 12 2013 generator, FindGDAL, and CMakeFindFrameworks, and the parser does not emit those declarations yet, so they produce no finding.
- Conan and vcpkg packages, language standards, compilers, and baselines with no rule. A missing finding is not evidence that a version is current.
- `cmake_minimum_required` written as a policy range (`VERSION 3.5...3.16`), a value read from a variable, or a generator expression.
- Conan `[tool_requires]` and `[build_requires]`, version ranges, and dynamic Python.
- Feature-scoped vcpkg dependencies and `overrides`.
- Vulnerability advisories and license policy.

### Known limits and false-positive boundaries

- A `version>=` floor is matched as that version, not as every version the constraint allows. A floor inside a rule is reported even when a newer resolution would sit outside it.
- A compiler check matches the compared version. `VERSION_LESS 9.3` is not read as "this project rejects compilers older than 9.3."
- A baseline commit matches a rule that covers every version, because that range does not inspect the commit.
- Malformed input produces no declarations from that file, never a partial result, and no error is raised. A file over 1 MiB yields nothing, and a single line over 4,096 characters is skipped.
- The eight-level and 500-file limits are silent. Files beyond them, and any under `build`, `vendor`, or another skipped directory, are not scanned.

## Serverless runtimes detector

The `serverless` detector is **beta**: its level is recorded as `beta` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`, and the precision floor is enforced. Ten public repositories in [Validation](VALIDATION.md#serverless-corpus) cover it (five targeted, five blind). Supported forms, limits, and data sources are documented in [Serverless runtimes](detectors/serverless.md). Its lifecycle rules are in `registry/serverless.json` and ship in the [data bundle](DATA.md).

## Android detector

The `android` detector is **experimental**: its level is recorded as `experimental` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`. Five public repositories are pinned for it in `benchmarks/public-repositories.json` (four targeted, one blind). Its lifecycle rules are in `registry/android.json` and ship in the [data bundle](DATA.md). The bundled rules cover Google Play Billing Library majors 5 through 9 and cite the [Google Play Billing Library version deprecation](https://developer.android.com/google/play/billing/deprecation-faq) timeline. Scans read that bundled registry only.

### Supported files and declarations

| File | Declaration read | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts` | Literal `compileSdk`, `minSdk`, `targetSdk`, and `buildToolsVersion` inside an `android { }` block, including `defaultConfig`, product flavors, and build types | An API level is a bare or quoted integer (`34`, `"34"`, `= 34`). `buildToolsVersion` is a quoted dotted number (`"34.0.0"`). |
| `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts` | A string-notation Maven coordinate on `implementation`, `api`, `compileOnly`, `runtimeOnly`, `testImplementation`, `testRuntimeOnly`, `testCompileOnly`, `annotationProcessor`, `kapt`, `ksp`, `compile`, `runtime`, or `testCompile` | The form is `implementation("group:artifact:version")`, with or without the parentheses. An optional classifier or `@` packaging suffix is not part of the version. |
| `settings.gradle`, `settings.gradle.kts` | A literal `id(...) version "..."` pin (Groovy quotes work too) for `com.android.application`, `com.android.library`, or `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` | `apply false` still counts. The pin is read wherever it appears in the file. |
| `libs.versions.toml` | `agp` and `kotlin` keys in the `[versions]` table, each a quoted literal version | The file is found by that name at any depth, including `gradle/libs.versions.toml`. |

Files are found by walking the repository up to eight directories deep, to at most 2,000 of these files. Symbolic links are not followed, and `.git`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, `.gradle`, `.venv`, `venv`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, and `testdata` are skipped. Gradle is never run, and nothing is fetched.

### Package URLs

A string-notation dependency `group:artifact:version` is `pkg:maven/<group>/<artifact>`. An SDK setting is `pkg:generic/android/compileSdk`, `pkg:generic/android/minSdk`, `pkg:generic/android/targetSdk`, or `pkg:generic/android/buildToolsVersion`. An Android Gradle Plugin pin, in settings or the catalog `agp` key, is `pkg:generic/android/agp`. `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` in settings is `pkg:generic/android/kotlin-android`. The catalog `kotlin` key is `pkg:generic/android/kotlin`, a different identity from the settings plugin.

### What it reports

- A string-notation `com.android.billingclient:billing` version that a bundled rule contains. The rules cover majors 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9.
- An SDK level, Android Gradle Plugin version, Kotlin Android plugin version, or catalog `agp` / `kotlin` pin when a rule for that Package URL contains the version text. No such rules are bundled, so those declarations produce no finding today.

The first matching rule wins. A rule whose VERS is malformed, or whose comparison throws, is skipped and does not hide a later rule. Each finding names the file and line, and carries its rule's source, replacement, deadline, migration guidance, and verification commands. A rule that lists usage matchers also lists `.java` and `.kt` usages. The bundled Play Billing rules do not list matchers, so those findings point at the declaration only.

### What it intentionally does not judge

- SDK levels, plugin versions, catalog pins, and Maven coordinates with no rule in `registry/android.json`. A missing finding is not evidence that a version meets Google Play's target API requirement or that a dependency is current.
- JDK pins in the same Gradle file (`sourceCompatibility`, `targetCompatibility`, `jvmToolchain`, `JavaLanguageVersion`). The Java and Kotlin detector reads those.
- Legacy names `compileSdkVersion`, `minSdkVersion`, and `targetSdkVersion`, method calls such as `compileSdk(34)`, and receiver forms such as `ext.minSdk`.
- Values outside an `android { }` block, property references, version-catalog calls, and `$` interpolation.
- Plugin versions written in `build.gradle(.kts)`, `alias(libs.plugins…)` lines, `kotlin("android") version "…"`, the chained `id("…").version("…")` form, and plugin ids other than `com.android.application`, `com.android.library`, and `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android`.
- Catalog keys other than `agp` and `kotlin`, and any version outside `[versions]`, including a `[plugins]` `version` or `version.ref`.
- Map notation (`group:`, `name:`, `version:`), version-catalog library aliases such as `implementation(libs.billing)`, and configuration names outside the list above, such as `debugImplementation` and `androidTestImplementation`.
- Dynamic and ranged versions (`8.+`, `latest.release`, `[8.0, 9.0)`) on plugin and catalog pins.
- Vulnerability advisories and license policy.

### Known limits and false-positive boundaries

- A literal inside `android { }` is reported when a rule matches it, including a product flavor or build type, and including a script the project no longer applies. Evergreen does not ask Gradle which variant is live.
- A plugin pin is read anywhere in `settings.gradle(.kts)`, including `pluginManagement` and a line marked `apply false`.
- String-notation test configurations are judged the same way as `implementation`.
- A catalog `kotlin` pin and the settings Kotlin Android plugin do not share a Package URL. A rule for one does not match the other.
- An unterminated comment or string, or a Kotlin string template the scanner cannot pair, makes that parser return nothing for the whole file. A `libs.versions.toml` with a multi-line string (`"""` or `'''`) does the same.
- Malformed input produces no declarations from the affected file, never a partial result, and no error is raised. A file over 1 MiB yields nothing, and a single line over 4,096 characters is skipped. Each parser keeps at most 5,000 declarations from one file.
- The eight-level and 2,000-file limits are silent. Files beyond them, and any under `build`, `.gradle`, or another skipped directory, are not scanned.
- A plugin or catalog value that is not a literal version is omitted. A string-notation coordinate is kept and compared as the version text written in the file. The analysis reports no unclassified references.

## CI runner images detector

The `ci-images` detector is **experimental**: its level is recorded as `experimental` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`. Five targeted public repositories are pinned for it (see [VALIDATION.md](VALIDATION.md) "CI runner images corpus"); precision is not enforced, and its blind share is zero. Its lifecycle rules are in `registry/ci-images.json` and ship in the [data bundle](DATA.md). Bundled rules include the scheduled removals of the macOS 14 Sonoma and Ubuntu 22.04 hosted images, citing the [Microsoft-hosted image deprecation schedule](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted-deprecation-schedule). A label is a finding only when a reviewed rule covers it. Scans read that bundled registry only.

### Supported files and declarations

| File | Declaration read | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `azure-pipelines.yml` | Literal `pool.vmImage` on the pipeline, a stage, or a job | The label is matched when it is `ubuntu-<version>`, `macos-<version>`, or `windows-<version>`, compared case-insensitively. |
| `.gitlab-ci.yml` | Root and job `image` values, including an image object's `name`, and image values in `services` | Every located value is unclassified. None become findings. |
| `.circleci/config.yml` | `docker.image` and `machine.image` under `jobs` and `executors`, and string values under `orbs` | Orbs, dynamic values, and floating aliases are unclassified. A literal image is parsed and not judged. |

Only a file named `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, or `config.yml` directly inside a `.circleci` directory is read. Files are found by walking the repository up to eight directories deep, to at most 500 files. Symbolic links are not followed, and `.git`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `bin`, `obj`, `target`, `.venv`, `venv`, `fixtures`, `__fixtures__`, and `testdata` are skipped. GitLab CI, CircleCI, and Azure Pipelines are never run, and nothing is fetched.

### What it reports

- An Azure `pool.vmImage` whose family and numeric version a rule's Package URL and `vers` range contain. The finding is the value's line. It carries the rule's source, replacement, deadline, and migration guidance when the rule has it. Every matching rule is reported.
- Nothing for a GitLab image or service, a CircleCI image or orb, or an Azure label no rule covers. An unclassified reference is not a finding.

### What it intentionally does not judge

- GitLab CI images and services. Decision 0014 records no authoritative GitLab lifecycle source, so a literal image is not evidence that GitLab retired it.
- CircleCI `docker.image` and `machine.image` values, including ones that look old. This version has no CircleCI Package URL mapping, so a literal image is not matched against a rule. Orb references are not image lifecycle claims, and their remote contents are not read.
- `latest`, `ubuntu-latest`, `macos-latest`, `windows-latest`, and other `*-latest` or `:latest` aliases. `cimg/<name>:current` is floating too.
- Dynamic values: `$IMAGE`, `${IMAGE}`, `$(vmImage)`, `<< parameters.image >>`, `<< pipeline.parameters.image >>`, and any value that contains `$` or `<<`.
- Azure labels outside `ubuntu-`, `macos-`, and `windows-` plus a numeric version, including `ubuntu-22.04-arm64` and `windows-2025-vs2026`.
- A pool written as a string, a pool `name` without `vmImage`, containers, resources, and `strategy.matrix` `vmImage` entries.
- CircleCI workflow executor references, `resource_class`, descriptions, and a job that only names an orb executor.
- Comments, unrelated keys, unresolved YAML aliases, merge keys, non-string values, and malformed YAML.
- Vulnerability advisories. A newer image existing is not a lifecycle finding.

### Known limits and false-positive boundaries

- An Azure label is reported when a rule matches the text, including a pipeline the project no longer runs, and including a self-hosted agent that reuses a hosted label string. Evergreen does not ask Azure DevOps which pipeline is active.
- GitLab and CircleCI references that are unclassified name the file and line. A literal CircleCI image is omitted from both findings and unclassified references.
- Malformed YAML produces no declarations from that file, never a partial result, and no error is raised. A file over 1 MiB yields nothing, and a single value over 4,096 characters is skipped.
- The eight-level and 500-file limits are silent. Files beyond them, and any under a skipped directory, are not scanned.

## Monorepos

The npm and Python detectors read every package of a workspace, not only the repository root. Packages are found from the declarations the package managers use: `workspaces` in `package.json` (npm and Yarn, array or `packages` form), `pnpm-workspace.yaml` (with `!` exclusions), `lerna.json`, and `[tool.uv.workspace]` `members` and `exclude` in `pyproject.toml`. Globs support `*`, `?`, and `**`.

- Findings name the package's own file, for example `packages/a/package.json`, and carry the usages inside that package's directory; usages outside every package stay with the root.
- A workspace without its own lockfile resolves versions against the root's lockfile.
- Discovery is bounded: eight directory levels, 500 packages, symbolic links never followed, and `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `target`, virtual environments, and fixture directories skipped.
- A malformed workspace manifest is skipped, so one bad package does not hide the others. A malformed root `package.json` is still an error.
- Without a workspace declaration only the root is scanned, as before. Python projects that are not uv workspaces (for example separate `pyproject.toml` files under `services/`) are not discovered.

## CI behavior

- In GitHub Actions, the doctor requires `GITHUB_WORKSPACE` to name an accessible
  checkout directory.
- In GitLab CI, the doctor requires `CI_PROJECT_DIR` to name an accessible checkout
  directory.
- Outside those environments, it reports local execution and does not require CI
  variables.

The checks only read Evergreen's own packaged metadata and test workspace
accessibility. They do not inspect secrets, tokens, repository contents, or remote
services.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/AGENT_SKILLS.html

# Evergreen Agent Skill

Evergreen ships one portable skill at `skills/evergreen-deprecation/SKILL.md`. It follows the open Agent Skills directory format: standard YAML frontmatter plus Markdown instructions. There is no vendor-specific manifest, invocation policy, tool allowlist, script, or generated prompt.

## Design

The skill is intentionally an orchestration layer. It tells an agent when to discover, explain, migrate, and verify, then maps those intents to Evergreen's MCP tools or CLI commands. Lifecycle rules, evidence, affected-file calculation, migration steps, and verification behavior remain in the executable and versioned JSON contracts.

This split prevents prompt drift: improving a detector or migration packet changes every client without requiring a rewritten skill.

## Installation

The skills CLI discovers the Skill directly from the Evergreen monorepo. No dedicated distribution repository is needed:

```sh
npx skills add arminazimi/evergreen
```

The repository currently exposes one Skill. For a non-interactive or explicitly selected install, use:

```sh
npx skills add arminazimi/evergreen --skill evergreen-deprecation --yes
```

Update it with:

```sh
npx skills update evergreen-deprecation
```

The npm package also includes the complete `skills/evergreen-deprecation` folder for hosts that prefer a manual copy or link.

The host also needs one Evergreen execution path:

- the local `evergreen-mcp` stdio server; or
- the `evergreen` CLI available on `PATH`.

No account or API key is required.

## Discovery and host compatibility

On 2026-10-15, `npx skills add arminazimi/evergreen --list` discovered exactly one Skill named `evergreen-deprecation`. A clean project installation then selected and installed that Skill for five representative skills CLI targets:

| Host | `--agent` value | Install result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex | `codex` | Passed |
| Claude Code | `claude-code` | Passed |
| Cursor | `cursor` | Passed |
| GitHub Copilot | `github-copilot` | Passed |
| Gemini CLI | `gemini-cli` | Passed |

The same install registered the Skill with skills.sh. It is discoverable as `arminazimi/evergreen@evergreen-deprecation` at [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/arminazimi/evergreen/evergreen-deprecation). The skills CLI security summary reported Gen Agent Trust Hub **Safe**, Socket **0 alerts**, and Snyk **Low Risk** at validation time. These external assessments can change and do not replace review of the installed files.

## Evaluation

Trigger evaluation cases live in `skills/evergreen-deprecation/evals/cases.json`. The versioned corpus contains 60 prompts: 30 expected triggers and 30 expected non-triggers, including 12 deliberately ambiguous requests. Each of the `agent-skills`, `codex`, and `claude` discovery lanes has 20 cases with an even positive/negative split.

Run the deterministic metadata-selection proxy from the repository root:

```sh
npm run eval:skill-triggers
```

The command builds the evaluator, prints JSON results overall and by host lane, lists any failed case IDs, and exits unsuccessfully when the corpus has fewer than 50 cases, recall is below 90%, or the false-trigger rate is 5% or higher. It has no model, network, account, or API-key dependency, so CI and contributors can reproduce the same baseline.

Current published baseline:

| Lane | Cases | Recall | False-trigger rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All | 60 | 100% | 0% |
| Agent Skills | 20 | 100% | 0% |
| Codex | 20 | 100% | 0% |
| Claude | 20 | 100% | 0% |

This is a contract test for the concepts exposed by the skill metadata, not a claim that every model version will make an identical routing decision. Live host checks can add observations without weakening the deterministic CI gate. Generic dependency upgrades, vulnerability or security audits, deprecated application APIs, and unrelated modernization are explicit negative cases.

### Dependency guard evaluation

The Skill also tells an agent to check a package, runtime, or action before adding it (`check_dependency` or `evergreen check`). `skills/evergreen-deprecation/evals/dependency-cases.json` measures that trigger: 48 prompts, 27 expected checks and 21 that should not trigger one, split evenly across the three discovery lanes. Positives add or choose a dependency in npm, PyPI, and GitHub Actions terms (`npm install request-promise`, `Add actions/checkout@v4 to the CI workflow`, `Which package should I use for date handling?`). Negatives are removals, installs of what the lockfile already declares, routine upgrades, `dependency injection`, tests, documentation, and refactors; six edge cases are labeled ambiguous with the decision and reason recorded.

`npm run eval:skill-triggers` reports recall and false-trigger rate for it under `dependencyGuard`, overall and by lane, with the same gates (at least 40 cases, recall of 90% or more, false-trigger rate under 5%). Like the lifecycle evaluation it is a deterministic proxy for what the Skill metadata says, not a measurement of any particular model; live runs in each host can add observations without weakening the gate.

CI also validates the portable frontmatter, small instruction surface, vendor neutrality, complete tool mapping, and safety invariants.

Independent forward tests exercise three different agent situations:

| Agent situation | Observable success criterion | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Skill discovery | Classify every trigger and non-trigger case through the metadata contract without reading expected answers. | 60/60 correct across three lanes. |
| MCP-capable agent | Discover, explain, create context, migrate, and verify through the real stdio protocol in one session. | Passed with all five tools; checkout finding verified absent. |
| CLI-only agent | Complete the same lifecycle using only documented CLI fallbacks and a fresh final scan. | Passed; request migration changed only two packet files and ended with zero findings. |

Forward-test observations are recorded on the Week 11 GitHub issue when the phase is completed. Discovery testing narrowed an ambiguous generic migration trigger to migrations from Evergreen findings. CLI testing replaced the packet's `npx` rescan suggestion with the already-installed `evergreen` executable so verification remains offline-capable and version-consistent. MCP testing clarified that an empty usage list means there are no additional usages beyond the declaration, rather than implying that the declaration itself is not relevant.

## Limits and security assumptions

- Evergreen currently covers its documented GitHub Actions, Node.js, npm, and Python rules. The skill reports unsupported ecosystems instead of inventing migration advice.
- Dynamic references that detectors cannot classify remain explicit limitations.
- MCP verification needs the same server session that observed the finding. The CLI fallback uses a fresh scan and conservatively compares the rule and declaration path.
- The skill grants no permissions. Suggested verification commands remain subject to the host's normal authorization rules.
- The bundle contains no executable skill scripts and declares no pre-approved tools.
- Installing through the skills CLI copies or links instruction files into the selected host's Skill directory; it does not install the Evergreen runtime itself.
- Repository analysis remains local. The selected host receives structured Evergreen results, which can include paths and short source excerpts, so its own privacy policy still applies.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/RULES.html

# Lifecycle rules

Every lifecycle claim Evergreen makes comes from a rule in `registry/`. A rule says which component is affected, in which versions, what happened to it, who says so, and when that was last checked. This page is the reference for writing one.

The format is `evergreen.registry.v2`. Its JSON Schema is [`schemas/registry.v2.schema.json`](../schemas/registry.v2.schema.json), and the reasoning is in [Decision 0004](decisions/0004-registry-v2.md). All five bundled registries (`container`, `github-actions`, `nodejs`, `npm`, `python`) use it.

## A complete rule

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "evergreen.registry.v2",
  "ecosystem": "npm",
  "freshness": { "maxReviewAgeDays": 365 },
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "npm.package.request.deprecated",
      "ecosystem": "npm",
      "purl": "pkg:npm/request",
      "vers": "vers:npm/*",
```
