```json
      "event": "deprecated",
      "title": "request is deprecated",
      "summary": "The package is fully deprecated and no new changes are expected.",
      "severity": "high",
      "replacement": "Native fetch or a maintained HTTP client",
      "deadline": "2020-02-11",
      "sources": [
        { "title": "request package deprecation notice", "url": "https://www.npmjs.com/package/request" }
      ],
      "provenance": {
        "observedAt": "2026-10-13",
        "reviewedAt": "2026-10-14",
        "reviewer": "arminazimi"
      },
      "migration": {
        "constraints": ["Preserve request method, headers, authentication, redirects, and error semantics at each call site."],
        "steps": [
          { "id": "replace-request-calls", "title": "Rewrite request usages", "instructions": "Translate each reported import and call to native fetch or a maintained client.", "targets": "usages" }
        ],
        "verification": [
          { "command": "npm run test --if-present", "purpose": "Run the repository tests when defined." }
        ]
      },
      "usage": [
        { "kind": "import", "language": "javascript", "module": "request" }
      ],
      "x-npm": { "package": "request" }
    }
  ]
}
```

A second, smaller example lives in [`examples/registry.v2.example.json`](../examples/registry.v2.example.json). The bundled files in `registry/` are the best reference for each ecosystem.

## The registry file

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `schemaVersion` | yes | Always `evergreen.registry.v2`. |
| `ecosystem` | yes | A lowercase slug such as `npm`. Every rule in the file must use the same value. |
| `freshness.maxReviewAgeDays` | no | How long a rule may go without review before the weekly check reports it stale. Defaults to 365. |
| `rules` | yes | The rules, in the order detectors should consider them. |

## A rule

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | yes | Stable and unique, lowercase with dots and hyphens, for example `npm.package.request.deprecated`. Baselines and reports refer to it, so do not rename it. |
| `ecosystem` | yes | Matches the registry's `ecosystem`. |
| `purl` | yes | The affected component as a [Package URL](https://github.com/package-url/purl-spec), canonical and **without a version**: `pkg:npm/request`, `pkg:npm/%40angular/core`, `pkg:pypi/django-nose`, `pkg:github/actions/checkout`. Runtimes with no registry use `pkg:generic/<name>`, for example `pkg:generic/nodejs`. |
| `vers` | yes | The affected versions as a [VERS](https://github.com/package-url/vers-spec) range, for example `vers:npm/*` (every version), `vers:semver/<5.0.0`, `vers:semver/>=20.0.0\|<21.0.0`, `vers:pypi/<3.10`. Write it in canonical form: no spaces, no explicit `=`, constraints sorted by version. |
| `event` | yes | What happened, or what has been announced: `deprecated`, `end-of-support`, `end-of-life`, `removed`, or `scheduled-end-of-life`. Use the word the source uses; see [Choosing an event](#choosing-an-event). |
| `title` | yes | One line that names the problem. |
| `summary` | yes | One or two sentences stating what the source says, without advice. |
| `severity` | yes | `info`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `critical`. |
| `replacement` | no | What to move to. |
| `deadline` | no | The date from the source, as `YYYY-MM-DD`. Omit it when the source gives none. |
| `sources` | yes | At least one authoritative source, each with a `title` and an `https` `url` (and optionally `accessedAt`). |
| `provenance` | yes | See below. |
| `migration` | no | Constraints, ordered steps, and verification commands. Used by `evergreen context`. Step `targets` are `declaration`, `usages`, or `all`; step ids are unique within the rule. |
| `usage` | no | Imports, calls, configuration keys, and deprecated symbols that show where a repository depends on the component. See [Symbol-level usage](#symbol-level-usage). |
| `x-<ecosystem>` | no | Matching hints the ecosystem's detector reads, such as `x-npm.package`, `x-nodejs.major`, `x-python.kind`, or `x-github-actions.supportedFromMajor`. See [Detector hints](#detector-hints). |

### Symbol-level usage

A `usage` entry of kind `symbol` marks one deprecated function, method, class, or option inside a module, so a rule can say `ReactDOM.render` is deprecated without flagging all of `react-dom`. `purl` and `vers` still say which package versions are affected; the entry says which symbol.

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | yes | `symbol`. |
| `language` | yes | `javascript`, `typescript`, or `python`. Write one entry per language. |
| `module` | no | The module that exports the symbol, as it is imported: `react-dom`, `datetime`. Omit it for globals and builtins such as `Buffer` or `open`. |
| `symbol` | yes | Dotted path from the module: `render`, `Buffer.alloc`, `datetime.utcnow`. Identifier segments only. |
| `shape` | yes | How the symbol is used: `call`, `construct` (`new X()`, JavaScript and TypeScript only), `reference` (any other use, such as passing it as a value), or `option` (a deprecated property in the call's options object). |
| `option` | when `shape` is `option` | The deprecated property name. Not allowed for other shapes. |
| `argument` | no | For `option`: zero-based position of the options argument. Defaults to the last argument. |
| `replacement` | no | What to use instead of this symbol. It overrides the rule's `replacement` in reports. |

Symbol entries are read by parser-backed usage analysis. Regex-based analysis ignores them, so a rule that has only symbol entries reports the declaration but no usages until that analysis runs. Add an `import` entry for the module as well when you want the regex scanner to find it. A hit is reported as a usage of kind `symbol` at the first identifier of the name (at the property name for `option`), with the module and symbol as its `symbol` text, such as `fs.exists` or `fs.rmdir(recursive)`. Names are followed through imports, `require`, destructuring, aliases, and a `node:` prefix, and a global such as `Buffer` is not reported when the file imports or declares that name itself. Scopes are not modelled, so a local variable that shadows an imported name can be reported. For Python, an `option` matches a keyword argument anywhere in the call, or a positional argument at `argument`. Each symbol entry needs its own evidence: the rule's `sources` must name the symbol, not only the package.

A complete rule, also in [`examples/registry.v2.symbol.example.json`](../examples/registry.v2.symbol.example.json):

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": "evergreen.registry.v2",
  "ecosystem": "npm",
  "freshness": {
    "maxReviewAgeDays": 365
  },
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "npm.symbol.react-dom.render.deprecated",
      "ecosystem": "npm",
      "purl": "pkg:npm/react-dom",
      "vers": "vers:npm/>=18.0.0",
      "event": "deprecated",
      "title": "ReactDOM.render is deprecated",
      "summary": "React 18 deprecates ReactDOM.render; it runs the app in React 17 mode and logs a warning.",
      "severity": "medium",
      "replacement": "createRoot from react-dom/client",
      "sources": [
        {
          "title": "React 18 upgrade guide: react-dom render",
          "url": "https://react.dev/blog/2022/03/08/react-18-upgrade-guide"
        }
      ],
      "provenance": {
        "observedAt": "2026-10-19",
        "reviewedAt": "2026-10-19",
        "reviewer": "arminazimi"
      },
      "migration": {
        "constraints": [
          "Keep the application's root container and rendered tree unchanged."
        ],
        "steps": [
          {
            "id": "use-create-root",
            "title": "Switch to createRoot",
            "instructions": "Replace each reported render call with createRoot(container).render(element).",
            "targets": "usages"
          }
        ],
        "verification": [
          {
            "command": "npm run test --if-present",
            "purpose": "Run the repository tests when defined."
          }
        ]
      },
      "usage": [
        {
          "kind": "import",
          "language": "javascript",
          "module": "react-dom"
        },
        {
          "kind": "symbol",
          "language": "javascript",
          "module": "react-dom",
          "symbol": "render",
          "shape": "call",
          "replacement": "createRoot(container).render(element)"
        },
        {
          "kind": "symbol",
          "language": "typescript",
          "module": "react-dom",
          "symbol": "render",
          "shape": "call",
          "replacement": "createRoot(container).render(element)"
        }
      ],
      "x-npm": {
        "package": "react-dom"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

To add one: find the official deprecation notice for the symbol, copy the rule above, set `purl` and `vers` to the package versions the notice covers, write one `symbol` entry per language, and run `npm run check`.

#### Walkthrough: add a symbol rule

This example adds a rule for `fs.exists`, which Node.js documents as deprecated in favour of `fs.access` or `fs.stat`. Follow the same steps for any symbol.

1. **Find the evidence.** Open the official documentation of the symbol and look for a deprecation notice. Here it is the `fs.exists` entry in the Node.js `fs` documentation, which carries `Stability: 0 - Deprecated`. Note the URL; the rule cites it. Without an authoritative notice for this symbol there is no rule.
2. **Pick the module and the symbol path.** `module` is what code imports: `fs`. `symbol` is the dotted path inside it: `exists`. Do not put the module in the symbol.
3. **Pick the shape.** `fs.exists(path, callback)` is called, so `shape` is `call`. Use `construct` for `new Buffer(size)`, `reference` when merely passing the function around is the problem, and `option` for a deprecated property of an options object.
4. **Write one entry per language.** Node.js code is JavaScript or TypeScript, so write two `symbol` entries that differ only in `language`. Add an `import` entry for the module too if you want the regex scanner to point at the file.
5. **Write the rule.** Copy the complete rule above, then set `purl`, `vers`, `title`, `summary`, `replacement`, `sources`, and `provenance` from the notice. `summary` states what the source says; the advice goes in `replacement`.
6. **Write a fixture.** A fixture is a small source file with usages that must be reported and lookalikes that must not. Put the expected result in comments so a reviewer can read it without running anything:

   ```js
   const fs = require("fs");
   const { promisify } = require("util");

   fs.exists("a.txt", () => {});          // reported: call of fs.exists
   const { exists } = require("fs");
   exists("b.txt", () => {});             // reported: destructured binding of fs.exists
   const check = fs.exists;
   check("c.txt", () => {});              // reported: alias of fs.exists

   fs.existsSync("a.txt");                // not reported: a different symbol
   fs.access("a.txt", () => {});          // not reported: the replacement
   const text = "fs.exists is deprecated"; // not reported: a string
   // fs.exists("d.txt", () => {});       // not reported: a comment
   const exists2 = (name) => name;
   exists2("e.txt");                      // not reported: an unrelated function
   ```

   Cover at least one reported usage per shape the rule declares, one alias, and the lookalikes above. A lookalike that the analysis reports is a bug in the rule or the analysis; fix it before the rule merges.
7. **Check it.** Run `npm run check`. It validates the rule against the schema, including every symbol entry, and fails when the reference pages under `docs/rules/` have drifted (run `npm run build:reference` to regenerate them). Open the pull request with `Closes #<issue>` and link the deprecation notice.

### Provenance

Provenance makes a rule auditable.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `observedAt` | The date you last saw the claim at its source. |
| `reviewedAt` | The date a maintainer last checked the rule against its sources. It must not be earlier than `observedAt`. |
| `reviewer` | Who reviewed it. |
| `importer` | The importer that drafted the rule, when one did. Omit it for hand-written rules. |

Dates are real calendar dates written `YYYY-MM-DD`; timestamps are rejected.

### Choosing an event

| Event | Use it when the source says |
|---|---|
| `deprecated` | The maintainer deprecated it, or put it in maintenance mode and recommends something else. |
| `end-of-support` | The release or version no longer receives support, for example because its runtime is gone. |
| `end-of-life` | The project or release line has reached end of life, is unmaintained, or is archived. |
| `removed` | The component, release, or service has been retired and no longer works. |
| `scheduled-end-of-life` | The vendor has announced a future end of life or end of support, with a date. The rule needs that date as its `deadline` and `severity: low`. It names the affected versions exactly as the later end-of-support or end-of-life rule will. When the date has passed, a reviewed change turns it into that rule (same `id`). See [decision 0010](decisions/0010-scheduled-end-of-life.md). |

If the source's wording fits two events, use the earlier one and quote the source in `summary`.

## Evidence policy

- Every rule needs an authoritative, versioned source: maintainer release notes, an official support or end-of-life policy, a registry deprecation flag, or platform documentation.
- Never infer lifecycle status from popularity, download counts, or a newer version existing.
- Dates, affected versions, and replacements must match the source. If the source is ambiguous, say so in the pull request.
- Rules are reviewed data, not code. Changes to `registry/` and `schemas/` are reviewed by a maintainer (see `.github/CODEOWNERS`).

## Validation

Everything above is enforced when a registry loads, and `npm run check` runs it on the bundled files. Validation reports every problem at once and names the rule and field, for example:

```text
Invalid registry (2 problems):
- rule "npm.package.request.deprecated": provenance.reviewedAt is required
- rule "npm.package.left-pad.deprecated": purl must be canonical and version-less (expected "pkg:npm/left-pad")
```

Beyond the schema, validation checks that:

- `purl` is canonical and has no version, qualifiers, or subpath;
- `vers` is canonical, its scheme is supported, every version in it is valid for that scheme, and the scheme fits the PURL type (for example `pypi` ranges on `pkg:pypi`);
- ids are unique, the rule's `ecosystem` matches the registry's, and there are no unknown fields (extensions must be named `x-<name>`);
- `migration` and `usage` entries are valid.

Supported version schemes are `semver`, `npm`, `cargo`, `golang`, `composer` (Semantic Versioning), `pypi` (PEP 440), `maven`, `nuget`, `gem`, and `intdot`.

## Freshness and sources

Scans never check freshness and never use the network, so results stay deterministic. A weekly workflow, [`.github/workflows/sources.yml`](../.github/workflows/sources.yml), runs `tools/check-sources.ts` and reports, separately:

- **stale** rules, reviewed longer ago than their `freshness.maxReviewAgeDays`;
- **changed** sources, whose final URL or title differs from the one recorded in `registry/sources.lock.json`;
- **unreachable** sources;
- **blocked** sources behind a bot challenge, which cannot be verified;
- **unrecorded** sources, not in the lock yet.

The check never edits rules. When it reports something, review the source, update the rule and its `reviewedAt`, and refresh the lock:

```bash
npm run build
node dist/tools/check-sources.js --update-lock
```

Run it locally with `npm run check:sources`.

## Detector hints

Existing detectors read a few fields that are specific to their ecosystem. In v2 they sit under `x-<ecosystem>` and are merged into the rule when the registry loads, so a detector sees the same rule it always has.

| Registry | Hints |
|---|---|
| `npm` | `x-npm.package` |
| `nodejs` | `x-nodejs.major` for one release line, or `x-nodejs.maximumMajor` for every line up to and including it |
| `python` | `x-python.kind` (`runtime` with `maximumVersion` such as `"3.9"`, or `package` with `package`) |
| `github-actions` | `x-github-actions.action` and `x-github-actions.supportedFromMajor` |

The hints must agree with `purl` and `vers`: `x-npm.package` is the package in `pkg:npm/...`, and `x-github-actions.supportedFromMajor: 5` goes with `vers:semver/<5.0.0`. New detectors should not add hints that `purl` and `vers` can already express.

## Drafting rules from sources

Rules do not have to be typed by hand. [Importers](IMPORTERS.md) read an authoritative source such as the Node.js release schedule or npm's deprecation flags and draft rules for you to review.

## Converting a v1 file

A tool converts registries written in the older, detector-specific format of the four bundled detectors. It derives `purl` and `vers` from the old fields, refuses to guess lifecycle events, and checks that every rule reads back unchanged:

```bash
npm run build
node dist/tools/registry-v1-to-v2.js registry/example.json \
  --observed-at 2026-10-13 --reviewed-at 2026-10-14 --reviewer your-name \
  --event example.rule.id=deprecated --out registry/example.json
```

## Detectors outside this repository

The public SDK still validates the v1 envelope (`validateRegistry`), so external detectors keep working unchanged. Loading v2 registries is currently internal to the bundled detectors; see [detector authoring](DETECTORS.md#registry-validation).

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/DATA.html

# Lifecycle data: updates, signing, and trust

Evergreen's findings come from lifecycle rules (`registry/`). The rules that ship inside each release are always available. Between releases you can fetch newer rules, which are signed so that Evergreen can tell they came from the project's release workflow. This page explains how that works, what is checked, and what Evergreen promises.

## What you can rely on

- **Scans never use the network.** A scan, `check`, `explain`, `context`, `baseline`, `doctor`, and `data status` read local files only. The only command that connects to anything is `evergreen data update`, and it runs only when you run it. A test fails if any other code path opens a socket, resolves a name, or calls `fetch`.
- **Downloaded data is verified before it is used, every time it is loaded.** If it cannot be verified, Evergreen uses the data shipped with the installed release and says so in the result. It never loads data it could not verify.
- **You can see how fresh the evidence is.** Every scan and check says which data it used and how old it is, and warns when that is more than 30 days.
- **You can fix the data version** for reproducible CI.
- **No account, no telemetry.** Updating asks a public release list and downloads public files. Nothing about you or your repository is sent.

## Commands

```bash
evergreen data status                       # which data is in use, where it came from, how old it is (--json for tools)
evergreen data update                       # fetch and verify the newest signed bundle
evergreen data update --data-version 2026.10.01   # fetch exactly that bundle, without making it active
evergreen scan . --data-version 2026.10.01  # use exactly that bundle (every command takes this)
EVERGREEN_DATA_VERSION=bundled evergreen scan .   # use only the data shipped with this release
```

`data status` reports one of three sources: **bundled** (shipped with the release), **cache** (the newest verified download), or **pinned** (the version you asked for). Its age is counted from when a downloaded bundle was built, or from the newest review date among the rules for bundled data.

### Updating

`evergreen data update` lists the project's `data-v…` releases, picks the newest one that has a bundle and a signature, downloads both (https only, with size limits and timeouts), verifies them completely, and only then stores them in your cache and makes them active. If anything is wrong the previous data stays active and nothing is written. Running it again when nothing changed says so.

It refuses a bundle that is older than the active one (a replayed old bundle would roll your rules back), a bundle the installed release already beats, and anything that fails verification. Three bundles are kept.

Downloads honor `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY` (Node.js 22.21 or newer). To use a mirror, point `EVERGREEN_DATA_URL` at its release list.

### Pinning

`--data-version X` or `EVERGREEN_DATA_VERSION=X` (the flag wins) makes Evergreen use exactly bundle `X` from your cache, or `bundled` for the data shipped with the release. Unlike the automatic choice, a pin that cannot be met **stops the run** with exit code 2 instead of quietly using something else, so a CI job that pins its data either uses it or fails. The message tells you how to fetch it: `evergreen data update --data-version X`. A pinned bundle is verified just like any other, and is used whatever its age (the stale warning still appears).

### Where the data is stored

`EVERGREEN_DATA_DIR` if set, otherwise `~/Library/Caches/evergreen` (macOS), `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/evergreen` or `~/.cache/evergreen` (Linux), or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\evergreen\Cache` (Windows). Inside, `data/<version>/` holds `bundle.json` and its signature `bundle.json.sigstore.json`, and `data/active.json` names the active version. Deleting the directory returns Evergreen to the bundled data.

## What is in a bundle

One JSON file (`evergreen.data-bundle.v1`, [schema](../schemas/data-bundle.v1.schema.json), [decision record](decisions/0006-data-bundle.md)) with a manifest and the files the detectors read: the five registries (container images, GitHub Actions, Node.js, npm, Python) and the GitHub Actions SHA map. The manifest lists each file's SHA-256, size, and rule count, a content address for the whole set, the build time, and the oldest Evergreen version that can read it. Versions look like `2026.10.16`, with `.N` for a second bundle on the same day. Building the bundle is deterministic: the same registry files and build time give the same bytes.

## Trust model

A bundle is signed with **Sigstore keyless signing**. There is no long-lived signing key to steal or lose: the release workflow proves who it is to Sigstore with a short-lived GitHub identity token, receives a certificate that lasts minutes, signs the bundle, and the signature is recorded in a public transparency log.

Evergreen accepts a bundle only if **all** of these hold, checked offline:

1. The signature verifies against the exact bytes downloaded (certificate chain, validity period, transparency-log inclusion).
2. The signer is the project's release workflow: issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` and an identity matching

   ```text
   ^https://github\.com/arminazimi/evergreen/\.github/workflows/data-release\.yml@refs/(?:tags/data-v\d{4}\.\d{2}\.\d{2}(?:\.\d+)?|heads/main)$
   ```

   A valid signature from any other workflow, repository, or branch is refused.
3. The format is one Evergreen understands and its `minimumEvergreenVersion` is not newer than the installed release.
4. The bundle is complete, and every file matches its digest and size, with nothing missing or extra.

The certificates and log keys come from the Sigstore public-good trusted root, which ships in the npm package (`data/sigstore-trusted-root.json`) so that verification needs no network. That is also why you should keep Evergreen reasonably current: if Sigstore rotates its keys and the root in your installed release is too old, signatures made after the rotation stop verifying. Evergreen then falls back to its bundled data and tells you; it does not skip the check.

To check a release by hand with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/):

```bash
cosign verify-blob \
  --bundle evergreen-data-2026.10.16.json.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/arminazimi/evergreen/\.github/workflows/data-release\.yml@refs/(?:tags/data-v\d{4}\.\d{2}\.\d{2}(?:\.\d+)?|heads/main)$' \
  evergreen-data-2026.10.16.json
```

### What this does not protect against

- A compromise of the repository's release workflow or of a maintainer with permission to push a `data-v…` tag: the workflow would sign whatever it was given. Rule changes are reviewed before they reach `main`, and the signature proves where a bundle came from, not that its contents are correct.
- A compromised Evergreen package: the trusted root and the signer identity are part of the release you installed.
- Wrong evidence. Signing says who published a rule, not that the claim is true; each rule cites its sources and review date for that reason.

## When something is wrong

Evergreen reports every refusal in the result, in the scan's `diagnostics` and in `data status`, for example:

```text
Ignoring downloaded lifecycle data 2026.10.16: registry/npm.json does not match its digest. Using the data bundled with Evergreen 0.3.0.
```

Common causes are a damaged download (run `evergreen data update` again), a bundle that needs a newer Evergreen (upgrade), and an expired trust root (upgrade). Data that is merely old is not an error; it is flagged stale after 30 days, and `evergreen data update` is the remedy.

## Publishing a bundle

Maintainers push a `data-vYYYY.MM.DD` tag; see [Releasing](RELEASING.md#publishing-lifecycle-data). The workflow builds the bundle twice and requires identical bytes, signs it, verifies the signature, and attaches the bundle, the signature, and checksums to a GitHub release.

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/VALIDATION.html

# v0.1 validation

Evergreen v0.1 was validated on 2026-10-14 against 20 public repositories pinned to immutable commits: ten Node.js repositories, nine Python repositories, and one Node.js/GitHub Actions repository. The complete corpus and expected finding locations live in `benchmarks/public-repositories.json`; the executable harness is `benchmarks/public-repositories.ts`.

## Results

| Measure | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Repositories | 20 |
| Expected findings | 27 |
| True positives | 27 |
| False positives | 0 |
| False negatives | 0 |
| Precision | 1.0000 |
| Recall | 1.0000 |
| Median scan time | 8.19 ms |
| p95 scan time | 48.88 ms |
| Slowest scan | 49.73 ms |

Scan time measures only local Evergreen analysis after checkout. It excludes network and Git operations, which the harness reports separately as `checkoutMs` per repository and `medianCheckoutMs`, `p95CheckoutMs`, and `slowestCheckoutMs` in the summary, so Evergreen's own cost is never mixed with the time spent downloading a repository. The run used the development machine, so duration is a reference rather than a cross-machine guarantee.

## GitHub Actions corpus additions

The corpus has since grown to 30 repositories. The ten added entries are GitHub Actions repositories taken from reviewed migration commits (see [Mining migrations](../benchmarks/mining/queries.md)). Eight are pinned to the commit *before* a migration, where Evergreen must report exactly the workflow locations the migration changed, and two are pinned to the migration commit itself, where it must report nothing. Together they include reusable workflows (`Akenon-Studio/.github`) and SHA-pinned actions (`smartcrabai/paperhanger`, `openmcp-project/crossplane-headlamp-plugin`).

Every expected finding in these entries has `groundTruthSource.kind` set to `migration-commit` and links to the commit that fixed it; a test checks each link against `benchmarks/mining/review-log.json`. A SHA-pinned entry is only accepted as zero-finding after checking that no pinned reference carries a version comment below the rule's supported major, because Evergreen does not classify SHA pins yet and would otherwise hide a deprecated version. Across all 30 repositories the harness reports 48 expected findings, 48 true positives, and no false positives or false negatives (observed 2026-10-16). The table above is the original 20-repository v0.1 run.

## Method

Every expected result is identified by rule ID, repository-relative path, and line at a pinned commit. The harness downloads each commit to a temporary directory, runs all built-in detectors, compares sets in both directions, reports per-repository timing, and removes the checkout. It exits unsuccessfully for any unexpected or missing finding.

```bash
npm run validate:public-repos
```

The audit covers both positive and zero-finding repositories across npm/Node.js, Python, and GitHub Actions. Findings were checked against their repository declarations and the authoritative sources bundled with the matching lifecycle rule.

## The 50-repository corpus

The corpus now has 50 repositories: the 20 from v0.1, the ten GitHub Actions entries above, and twenty more across the shipped detectors.

- Sixteen are pinned to the parent of a reviewed migration commit: six clean ones where the migration explains every finding (node-sass removals, Python runtime floors raised to a supported release), and ten where other deprecated declarations were still present. Findings that the migration fixed cite it with `groundTruthSource.kind` `migration-commit`; the rest are `maintainer-review` and quote the exact line that was read at that commit.
- Four are zero-finding repositories, including monorepos (`withastro/astro`, `vitest-dev/vitest`, `lerna/lerna`, `changesets/changesets`). They were also searched by hand for deprecated actions, runtimes and packages, independently of Evergreen's own rules.

The review tool (`benchmarks/mining/review.ts`) now accepts npm package, Python package, and Node.js and Python runtime rules as well as GitHub Actions rules, and `mine.ts` can mine one group at a time and append without replacing reviewed candidates (`--queries npm,python --limit 10 --append`). Across all 50 repositories the harness reports 81 expected findings, 81 true positives, no false positives and no false negatives (observed 2026-10-16).

## Kubernetes corpus

Five public repositories at pinned commits cover the `kubernetes` detector: `argoproj/argocd-example-apps` (Helm and kustomize applications, no findings), `kelseyhightower/ingress-with-static-ip`, `unixhot/salt-kubebin` (a CronJob and three Ingresses), `kubernetes/examples` (two PodSecurityPolicy documents, plus the two end-of-life base images the container detector reports there), and `lusyoe/springboot-k8s-example` (a Helm template and a plain manifest).

Because the corpus scans every detector, every finding in these repositories is recorded, not only the Kubernetes ones. Each expected finding was checked by reading its line at the pinned commit, and its `groundTruthSource` is a `maintainer-review` note naming the path and line; none of these repositories has a migration commit for the finding, so none is cited. The rules' dates and removal releases come from the Kubernetes migration guide, not from these repositories. A full run on 2026-10-17 over all 74 corpus entries (including the Java entries added in the next change) reported no false positives or false negatives, with nine expected `kubernetes` findings, all true.

## Java and Kotlin corpus

Five public repositories at pinned commits cover the `java` detector: `kagkarlsson/db-scheduler` (a multi-module Maven build, no findings), `piomin/sample-spring-reactive` (a `java.version` of 19), `danvega/loom` (`java.version`, `source`, and `target` of 19), `krakowski/jextract-demo` (a Gradle Kotlin DSL toolchain of 22), and `Descended/Henesys` (a `mysql:mysql-connector-java` 8.0.33 dependency, which the artifact's own POM relocates).

Every finding in these repositories is recorded, not only the Java ones, and each was checked by reading its line at the pinned commit. The ground truth is a `maintainer-review` note naming the path and line; none of the repositories has a migration commit for the finding. The JDK dates come from the Oracle Java SE Support Roadmap and the Temurin support page, and the relocation from the Maven Central POM, not from these repositories. A full run on 2026-10-17 over the 74 corpus entries then in the file reported no false positives or false negatives, with six expected `java` findings, all true.

## Swift corpus

Thirteen public repositories at pinned commits cover the `swift` detector.

Targeted: `seedco/Formalist` (`.xcode-version` 9.3.1 and an iOS 12 sample app), `bojan/Troop` (`.xcode-version` 10.2.1), `s2mr/xc` (`.xcode-version` 14.2.0), `s2mr/L10nLint` (`.xcode-version` 16.4.0), `Simperium/simperium-ios` (four iOS 8 application targets), and `JohnSundell/Files` (no findings).

Blind (rule below): `microsoft/SwiftStreamingMarkdown` (`.xcode-version` 16.0), `hhru/mvi-swift` (`.xcode-version` 16.0, plus `actions/checkout@v3` and Ruby 3.1), `babylonhealth/Stevenson` (`.xcode-version` 11.6), `cgoldsby/TvOSMoreButton` (`.xcode-version` 13.2.1, plus `actions/checkout@v2`, `actions/cache@v2`, and Ruby 2.7), `griffin-stewie/BudouX.swift` (`.xcode-version` 14.3.1), `micahflee/TM-SGNL-iOS` (no Swift finding: the pin reads `Xcode 16.1` and the app target is iOS 15; the same pin has `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/upload-artifact@v4`, and Ruby 3.2), and `paulgessinger/swift-paperless` (`.xcode-version` 27.1, no findings).

The Xcode acceptance dates come from [App Store upcoming requirements](https://developer.apple.com/news/upcoming-requirements/), not from these repositories.

## Swift blind selection

The six earliest Swift repositories were chosen knowing their result, so each records `selection: "targeted"`. The seven below record `selection: "blind"`.

The blind rule, fixed on 2026-10-21 before Evergreen ran on these additions: GitHub code search for `filename:xcode-version`. Walk unique repositories whose path is exactly `.xcode-version`, in the order returned that day. Skip a repository when it is a fork, archived, already in the corpus, not primarily Swift, or larger than 50,000 KB on GitHub. Keep it when the default branch still contains `.xcode-version`. Stop once the beta counts in [decision 0013](decisions/0013-detector-maturity.md) are met, which happened at seven. The seven, pinned at their default-branch commit on that date, are search results 12, 19, 20, 22, 24, 28, and 31: `paulgessinger/swift-paperless`, `microsoft/SwiftStreamingMarkdown`, `hhru/mvi-swift`, `babylonhealth/Stevenson`, `cgoldsby/TvOSMoreButton`, `micahflee/TM-SGNL-iOS`, and `griffin-stewie/BudouX.swift`. Results before and between those were skipped by the rule above (size, language, or an existing pin), including `signalapp/Signal-iOS`, `Simperium/simperium-ios`, and `seedco/Formalist`. The query returns different results on another day, so the pinned list above, not a re-run, is the record.

Ground truth: for each repository the `.xcode-version` line, every application-target `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`, and any other detector declaration on that pin were read from the file and compared with the report. `swift-paperless` pins Xcode 27.1, which neither Xcode rule covers, and its workflows are commit-pinned at majors the rules do not match, so the expected set is empty. `TM-SGNL-iOS` writes `Xcode 16.1`, which is not a numeric pin, and its application target is iOS 15, so the Swift detector reports nothing there; the Ruby pin and the Action refs are expected findings of those detectors. `BudouX.swift` pins `14.3.1`. Every expected finding has a `maintainer-review` note naming the path, the exact line, and the vendor date the rule rests on.

## Serverless corpus

Ten public repositories at pinned commits cover the `serverless` detector.

Targeted: `Dwolla/webhook-receiver` (`provider.runtime` `nodejs14.x`), `haltakov/natural-language-image-search` (`provider.runtime` `python3.8`), `HUK-COBURG/innoforum-aws-serverless` (SAM and Terraform `nodejs14.x`, plus GitHub Actions pins), `BaptisteLecat/gcp_architect_certification` (Terraform Google Cloud Functions `nodejs14`), and `aws-samples/sam-python-crud-sample` (five SAM `python3.8` functions, plus GitHub Actions pins).

Blind (rule below): `serverless/examples` and `AnomalyInnovations/serverless-stack-demo-api` (no findings), `Swizec/lambda-screenshot-as-a-service` (`nodejs14.x`), `skojin/send-gmail-lambda` (`ruby2.7`), and `livgust/covid-vaccine-scrapers` (seven SAM `nodejs14.x` functions, plus Node.js and GitHub Actions pins).

Because the corpus scans every detector, every finding in these repositories is recorded, not only the Serverless ones. Each expected finding was checked by reading its line at the pinned commit, and its `groundTruthSource` is a `maintainer-review` note naming the path and line; none of these repositories has a reviewed migration entry in the mining log for the finding, so none is cited as `migration-commit`. The AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Functions end-of-life dates come from the [AWS Lambda runtimes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtimes.html) table and the [Cloud Run functions runtime support](https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/runtime-support) schedule, not from these repositories.

## Serverless blind selection

The five earliest Serverless corpus repositories were chosen knowing their result, so each records `selection: "targeted"`. The five below record `selection: "blind"`.

The blind rule, fixed on 2026-10-21 before Evergreen ran on these additions: GitHub code search for `runtime: nodejs14.x` in `filename:serverless.yml`, plus the first results of `Runtime: nodejs14.x` / `Runtime: python3.8` in SAM `template.yaml` and of current `runtime: nodejs22.x` examples, walking public non-fork repositories in the order returned that day. Keep a repository when its default-branch tip contains `serverless.yml`, `template.yaml` / `template.yml`, or a Terraform `aws_lambda_function` / `google_cloudfunctions*_function` runtime declaration; skip archives and the repositories already pinned as targeted. Stop at five. The five, pinned at their default-branch commit on that date, are `serverless/examples`, `AnomalyInnovations/serverless-stack-demo-api`, `Swizec/lambda-screenshot-as-a-service`, `skojin/send-gmail-lambda`, and `livgust/covid-vaccine-scrapers`. The query returns different results on another day, so the pinned list above, not a re-run, is the record.

Ground truth: for each repository the runtime lines (and any other detector findings on the same pin) were listed by reading the pinned files and compared with the report, independently of Evergreen's own output. Every expected finding has a `maintainer-review` note naming the path, the exact line, and the vendor date the rule rests on.

## .NET blind selection

The six earliest .NET repositories were chosen knowing their result, so each records `selection: "targeted"`. The `selection` field is optional on every corpus entry; `"blind"` means the repository was chosen by a rule fixed before Evergreen ran on it ([decision 0013](decisions/0013-detector-maturity.md)), and an entry without the field counts as not blind.

The blind rule, run on 2026-10-19: GitHub repository search for `language:C#`, 100 to 500 stars, last pushed from 2021-01-01 to 2024-12-31, not a fork, not archived, sorted by stars descending (`gh search repos --language "C#" --stars "100..500" --updated "2021-01-01..2024-12-31" --archived=false --include-forks=false --sort stars --order desc`). Walk the results in order and take each repository whose default branch has at least one `*.csproj`, `*.fsproj`, `*.vbproj`, or `global.json`; skip the others (Unity packages with no project file). Stop at twelve, whatever Evergreen reports for them. The twelve, pinned at their default-branch commit on that date, are results 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16 of that search: rikimaru0345/Ceras, takuya-takeuchi/DlibDotNet, 0xthirteen/SharpStay, NightfallGT/Mercurial-Grabber, Dec0ne/ShadowSpray, Ceiridge/Chrome-Developer-Mode-Extension-Warning-Patcher, TerribleDev/OwinOAuthProviders, chsakell/mvcarchitecture, SeriaWei/ASP.NET-MVC-CMS, stanzhai/Html2Article, BeichenDream/SharpToken, and nettitude/SharpSocks. Ranks 2, 4, 6, and 8 have no project file. The query returns different results on another day, so the pinned list above, not a re-run, is the record.

Ground truth: for each repository the target frameworks, SDK pins, and package references were listed by `grep` over the pinned files and compared with the report, independently of Evergreen's own output. Every expected finding has a `maintainer-review` note naming the path, the exact line, and the vendor date the rule rests on. Ceras was the one miss: it targets `netcoreapp2.1` and `netcoreapp2.2`, which had no rule, so the registry gained the 1.x, 2.x, and 3.0 lines in the same change.

## CI runner images corpus

Five public repositories at pinned commits cover the `ci-images` detector: `oatpp/oatpp` (`ubuntu-20.04` and `ubuntu-22.04` hosted images), `Chinachu/Mirakurun` (four `ubuntu-22.04` pools, plus a deprecated `tslint` dependency), `microsoft/Sysmon-Linux` (`ubuntu-22.04`, plus `actions/checkout` v4.1.1), `aliostad/CacheCow` (`ubuntu-22.04`, plus .NET target frameworks past or scheduled for end of support), and `Windos/PoshNotify` (Azure Pipelines pools that use only `*-latest` images, no findings).

Because the corpus scans every detector, every finding in these repositories is recorded, not only the CI image ones. Each expected finding was checked by reading its line at the pinned commit, and its `groundTruthSource` is a `maintainer-review` note naming the path and line. The Azure dates come from the [hosted image deprecation schedule](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted-deprecation-schedule) and the [Azure DevOps blog deprecation plan](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/devops/upcoming-updates-for-azure-pipelines-agents-images/), not from these repositories. All five were chosen knowing their image labels, so each records `selection: "targeted"`.

## Precision thresholds

[`benchmarks/thresholds.json`](../benchmarks/thresholds.json) sets a precision floor per detector (`github-actions`, `nodejs`, `npm`, `python`, `dotnet`, `serverless`, and `swift` enforce it; a detector is named by the first segment of its rule ids). The harness scores each detector, prints the figures under `detectors` in its JSON, and reports `thresholdViolations`. A stable detector below its `minPrecision` (0.95 today) fails the run with a line such as:

```text
THRESHOLD  npm: precision 0.9 is below the required 0.95
```

The weekly corpus workflow therefore fails on a precision regression even if the exact-match comparison is later relaxed. Mark a new detector `"stable": false` until its corpus coverage is meaningful; it is still scored and reported but never fails the run. Never lower a floor to make a run pass.

## Fetching and the checkout cache

The harness fetches up to sixteen repositories at once; change that with `--concurrency <n>` or `EVERGREEN_CORPUS_CONCURRENCY`. Scans and the report stay in corpus order.

By default it fetches each repository as a blobless shallow fetch plus a sparse checkout of only the files the detectors declare they read ([decision 0015](decisions/0015-corpus-fetch-strategy.md)): a cold full run takes about a minute and fetches about 190 MB, and the results are identical to a full checkout. `EVERGREEN_CORPUS_FETCH=shallow` fetches complete checkouts instead. `node dist/benchmarks/fetch-strategies.js --strategy <shallow|sparse|tarball>` re-measures the options.

Every corpus commit is pinned, so a checkout never changes. Set `EVERGREEN_CORPUS_CACHE=<dir>` (for example `~/.cache/evergreen-corpus`) to keep each one on disk as `<owner>__<repo>@<commit>` and skip the network when it is already there. Entries are written to a temporary directory and renamed into place, and `.git` is removed because scans read files only, so an interrupted run never leaves a half-filled entry. A sparse entry carries an `.evergreen-fetch` marker naming the declarations it was built from; if a detector later declares more files, that entry is refetched rather than reused. Unset, there is no cache and a run behaves as before. A warm run reports the same true positives, false positives, false negatives, and findings as a cold one.

## Running a subset

```bash
npm run validate:public-repos -- --ecosystem php
npm run validate:public-repos -- --ecosystem php --ecosystem ruby
npm run validate:public-repos -- --repo laravel/framework
```

`--ecosystem <name>` and `--repo <owner/name>` are repeatable; naming both selects the union, reported in corpus order. An unknown name is an error that lists the valid ones. A filtered run still fails on any false positive or false negative among the entries it covers, but it is not a full run: it does not enforce the per-detector precision floors, it writes no `lastFullRun`, the JSON report says `"fullRun": false` with a `filter` line, and the run prints `FILTERED RUN` on stderr. Only an unfiltered run can be recorded or compared with the full-corpus claims in this document.

### Re-running only what failed

After fixing a detector, re-check just the repositories that had a mismatch:

```bash
npm run validate:public-repos -- --output corpus-result.json     # a run with UNEXPECTED or MISSING lines
npm run validate:public-repos -- --failed-from corpus-result.json
```

`--failed-from <report.json>` runs the repositories whose entry in that report has an `unexpected` or `missing` finding; any that have left the corpus are skipped. It is a filtered run like the others (`FILTERED RUN` on stderr, `"fullRun": false`) and never counts as a full run. A report with no mismatches prints that and exits 0 without fetching anything.

### Comparing with an earlier run

```bash
npm run validate:public-repos -- --compare corpus-result.json
npm run validate:public-repos -- --compare benchmarks/thresholds.json
```

`--compare <file>` prints what moved since that file. Against an earlier report it lists `ADDED` and `REMOVED` findings per repository and the per-detector true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative differences (`DELTA`), computed over the repositories present in both, so a filtered run compares like with like. Against `benchmarks/thresholds.json` it uses the recorded `lastFullRun` for the per-detector numbers only. Comparing never changes the exit code: false positives, false negatives, and the precision floors still decide it, and an unreadable comparison file is reported without failing the run.

### Managing the cache

A cache of complete checkouts is about 1.5 GB on disk; the default sparse entries need about 570 MB. A suggested location is `~/.cache/evergreen-corpus`; set `EVERGREEN_CORPUS_CACHE` to it in your shell profile.

```bash
npm run corpus:cache -- status                       # directory, entry count, total size, entries no longer in the corpus
npm run corpus:cache -- prune --dry-run              # what removing entries no longer in the corpus would do
npm run corpus:cache -- prune                        # remove entries that are no longer in the corpus
npm run corpus:cache -- prune --max-size 800         # remove least recently used entries until the cache is at most 800 MB
npm run corpus:cache -- prune --all                  # empty the cache
```

`--dry-run` works with every `prune` form and removes nothing. Every cache hit refreshes the entry's last-used time, which is what `--max-size` orders by. The commands only ever touch directories directly under the cache directory whose names look like `<owner>__<repo>@<40-hex commit>`; anything else in there is left alone, and an empty or root-like path (`/`, your home directory, a single top-level directory) is refused.

### Warm ahead, run offline

```bash
npm run corpus:warm                       # fetch every missing checkout into the cache and stop; no scan
npm run corpus:warm -- --ecosystem php    # the same filters as a run
npm run validate:public-repos -- --offline
```

Both need `EVERGREEN_CORPUS_CACHE` and print how many entries were already cached. `--offline` uses the cache only: if an entry is missing it fails before scanning anything, with exit code 2 and one message that lists every missing `repository@commit`. After `corpus:warm`, an `--offline` run reports the same results as an online one. A good habit is `npm run corpus:warm` after pulling `main`, so a later run never waits on a download.

### Running only what a change affects

```bash
npm run validate:public-repos -- --changed            # changes since origin/main, plus uncommitted and untracked files
npm run validate:public-repos -- --changed release/1  # a different base
```

`--changed [base]` reads `git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD` together with uncommitted and untracked files and maps them to corpus ecosystems with [`benchmarks/corpus-affected.ts`](../benchmarks/corpus-affected.ts): `src/detectors/<name>`, `registry/<file>.json`, and `tests/fixtures/<name>/` map to the ecosystems that detector serves (for example `src/detectors/npm.ts` and `registry/nodejs.json` to `node`, the GitHub Actions detector to `node-actions`), and shared files map to every ecosystem whose detectors use them (`src/source-usage.ts` to nine ecosystems; `src/engine.ts`, `src/sdk.ts`, and the other scan-wide files to all twelve). It prints one `changed:` line per chosen ecosystem naming the paths behind it. If nothing maps, it says so and exits 0 without fetching. The result is a filtered run like any other, and it combines with `--ecosystem` and `--repo`.

The map is tested: every built-in detector, every corpus ecosystem, every directory under `src/detectors/`, every file in `registry/`, and every shared file a detector imports must be listed, so adding a detector fails `npm run check` until it is mapped. Other work can import the same module, for example a pull request workflow.

## Run cost and budget

Every report carries a `cost` block: total wall time, the summed fetch time (larger than the wall time when fetches overlap), cache hits and misses, and the size of the git data fetched (git does not expose network bytes, so this is the `.git` size of each fetched checkout). The run prints it as a `COST` line, and the weekly workflow shows it in the job summary.

`benchmarks/thresholds.json` holds the `budget`: a wall-time limit in seconds and a fetched-bytes limit. Going over either prints a `BUDGET` warning (a `::warning::` annotation in Actions), lists it in the report's `budgetWarnings`, and flags it in the job summary. A budget overrun never fails the run; correctness is decided by false positives, false negatives, and the precision floors alone. Tighten the budget in a pull request when a faster fetch strategy lands, and raise it only with a stated reason.

## Stalled fetches

One hung connection must not hold a run. Each fetch passes git's low-speed abort (`http.lowSpeedLimit=1000`, `http.lowSpeedTime=30`: below 1 KB/s for 30 s) and a hard limit of 120 s per attempt, changed with `EVERGREEN_CORPUS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`. A stall counts as a failed attempt, so it is retried and, when every attempt fails, reported with the repository name. At the end of every run the five slowest fetches print as `SLOWEST` lines.

## Reading a run

By default a run prints a short table on stdout instead of the full JSON: true positives, false positives, false negatives, and precision per ecosystem and per detector, then every `UNEXPECTED` and `MISSING` line, then a one-line wall-time summary. Progress goes to stderr as one line per fetched repository (`12/107 owner/name 2.1s`). The `COST`, `SLOWEST`, and `BUDGET` lines follow on stderr.

```bash
npm run validate:public-repos -- --output corpus-result.json   # table on screen, full JSON in the file
npm run validate:public-repos -- --json > corpus-result.json   # JSON on stdout; the table moves to stderr
```

`--output <file>` writes the full JSON report whatever the result, so a failing run still leaves it behind. The weekly workflow uses `--output` and uploads that file as the `corpus-result-<run id>` artifact.

## Recording a full run

```bash
npm run record:corpus-run
```

One command replaces the hand edits. It runs the whole corpus in verify mode and, only when that passes, writes the run into `lastFullRun` in `benchmarks/thresholds.json` (date, the current `HEAD` commit, repository and finding counts, precision, recall, and true positives, false positives, and false negatives for every detector, zero for one that reported nothing), then regenerates `docs/dashboard/data.json` (`npm run build:dashboard`) and `docs/llms-full.txt`. It leaves the changes uncommitted so you can review the diff.

It refuses, and changes nothing, when:

- the working tree has uncommitted changes, because the recorded commit would not describe them;
- any run-narrowing flag is passed (`--ecosystem`, `--repo`, `--failed-from`, `--changed`), or `--observe`, `--warm`, `--output`, `--json`, or `--compare`;
- the run did not cover every corpus entry, was not in verify mode, or has any false positive or false negative, or a detector below its precision floor.

Other harness flags such as `--concurrency` and `--offline` are passed through. The dashboard tests read the recorded commit, counts, and age from `benchmarks/thresholds.json` instead of repeating them, so recording a new run needs no test edits.

## Pull request check

Pull request CI (`ci.yml`) stays offline, so a detector or rule change that adds false positives would only be found in the weekly run. [`.github/workflows/corpus-pr.yml`](../.github/workflows/corpus-pr.yml) closes that gap in a separate workflow: when a pull request touches `src/`, `registry/`, `tests/fixtures/`, or `benchmarks/`, it maps the changed files to corpus ecosystems with the same `--changed` logic described above and runs only those, using the weekly run's checkout cache (restore only).

The job summary lists the chosen ecosystems and every `UNEXPECTED` and `MISSING` line; the full report is attached as the `corpus-pr-result-<run id>` artifact. If nothing maps, it says so and fetches nothing. The workflow is **not a required check**: keep it out of branch protection, because it needs the network and GitHub's availability. It has `contents: read` only, no secrets, and no `pull_request_target`, and the base branch reaches the shell through an environment variable, never an inline expression. Treat a red run as a finding to explain in the pull request, using the rules in "Weekly run and refreshing pins" above.

## Weekly run and refreshing pins

Pull request CI never touches the network, so the corpus is checked by [`.github/workflows/corpus.yml`](../.github/workflows/corpus.yml) every Monday and on demand (Actions → Public corpus → Run workflow). The result is uploaded as the `corpus-result-<run id>` artifact even when the comparison fails. A failing run prints one line per mismatch, for example:

```text
UNEXPECTED owner/repo@4ec1ebe0fa: github-actions.setup-node.node20:.github/workflows/ci.yml:20
MISSING    owner/repo@4ec1ebe0fa: nodejs.runtime.eol-18:package.json:83
```

`UNEXPECTED` means Evergreen reported a finding the corpus does not list; `MISSING` means a listed finding was not reported. Because every commit is pinned, a mismatch means Evergreen's rules or detectors changed, not the repository. Decide which side is right before touching the corpus: fix the detector or rule when the corpus is right, and update the expected entry (with its `groundTruthSource`) only when the new result is correct.

To move an entry to a newer commit, change its `commit` to the full 40-character SHA, run `npm run observe:public-repos` to list what Evergreen now reports, review every difference against the repository at that commit, update `expected`, and run `npm run validate:public-repos` until it passes. Never refresh a pin only to make a failing run green.

## Differential testing against Renovate

Renovate is the closest widely used tool, so the report compares Evergreen's findings with Renovate's for the same repository, by rule family. A maintainer runs Renovate (it needs the network and a large download; it is not part of `npm run check` or any scan):

```bash
npx renovate --platform=local --dry-run=lookup --report-type=file --report-path=renovate.json
npm run differential:renovate -- --renovate renovate.json --repository . --name owner/repo --out report.json
```

The two tools answer different questions. Renovate says a newer version exists and prints npm deprecation notices; it has no end-of-life data. Evergreen says a release line is past its vendor's end of life; it does not say an update exists. So the report only compares where both can speak about one dependency in one file:

| Family | Evergreen | Renovate | Counted as agreement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `deprecated-package` | `npm.package.*` findings | npm `deprecationMessage` | both mark the package deprecated |
| `base-image` | `container.*` findings | `dockerfile` / `docker-compose` updates | Renovate offers an update for the image Evergreen calls end-of-life |
| `github-action` | `github-actions.*` findings | `github-actions` updates | Renovate offers an update for the action Evergreen flags |

Outcomes: `agree`, `evergreen-only`, `renovate-only`, and `inconclusive` (Renovate skipped the lookup, for example `github-token-required` for Actions when run without a GitHub token, so it says nothing either way). Runtime findings (`nodejs.runtime.*`, `python.runtime.*`) have no Renovate counterpart and are listed as not comparable. Matching is by file and dependency name because Renovate gives no line numbers.

Results for the five container corpus repositories, with Renovate 44.164 run without a GitHub token on 2026-10-16 (reports in [`benchmarks/differential/reports/`](../benchmarks/differential/reports/), trimmed Renovate output in `tests/fixtures/differential/`):

| Repository | Agree | Evergreen-only | Renovate-only | Inconclusive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| outline/outline | 2 | 0 | 17 | 15 |
| excalidraw/excalidraw | 3 | 0 | 2 | 20 |
| mealie-recipes/mealie | 3 | 0 | 4 | 14 |
| umami-software/umami | 2 | 0 | 2 | 4 |
| gethomepage/homepage | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

What it shows:

- **Agreements** are all base images: where Evergreen calls `node` or `postgres` end-of-life, Renovate offers a major update. Renovate does not say the old line is unsupported; only Evergreen does.
- **Renovate-only** are npm deprecations Evergreen has no rule for (for example `@types/*` stubs, `babel-eslint`, `koa-router`, `socket.io-redis`, `react-beautiful-dnd`, `rollup-plugin-terser`, `@nuxt/types`). This is the real gap: the `npm-deprecated` importer only checks a candidate list, so these names are candidates to add. Each is a Renovate observation, not evidence; the importer still requires the registry's own deprecation notice.
- **Evergreen-only** is empty here; every Evergreen finding that Renovate could look up, it also had an update for.
- Most GitHub Action findings are `inconclusive` because Renovate cannot look up Actions without a token. Re-run with `RENOVATE_TOKEN` to turn them into comparisons.

## Interpretation and limits

Precision and recall are measured only against Evergreen's documented v0.1 rule set and the pinned corpus. They do not mean Evergreen detects every possible deprecation in these ecosystems. The corpus is public and reproducible, but not a statistically representative sample of all software. Dynamic action references and unsupported ecosystems remain intentionally unclassified.

The controlled source-usage benchmark provides a separate exact-match test for imports, calls, and configuration keys; see [Benchmarks](BENCHMARKS.md).

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/PRIVACY.html

# Evergreen privacy

Evergreen analyzes software repositories on the user's computer. The Codex and Claude plugins start a local stdio MCP server and do not send repository contents to an Evergreen-operated service. Evergreen does not require an Evergreen account, collect analytics, use advertising identifiers, or sell personal data.

The local tools read supported manifests, lockfiles, workflow files, runtime-version files, and relevant source excerpts from the repository path the user authorizes. Results can contain file paths and short source excerpts. The host application receives those results, so its privacy policy and the user's workspace settings also apply.

The plugin launches the exact published `evergreen-deprecation` npm version recorded in its manifest. The package manager may contact the configured npm registry to obtain that package. Lifecycle evidence links are returned as references; Evergreen does not open them automatically.

Scans use no network. The one exception is `evergreen data update`, which you run yourself to fetch newer, signed lifecycle rules from the project's public GitHub releases. It sends nothing about you or your repository (a request for a public release list and two public files, which the host can see as it can any download), verifies the signature before using the data, and falls back to the rules shipped with the release if verification fails. See [Lifecycle data](DATA.md).

Evergreen's tools do not edit repository files, execute suggested migration commands, open a network listener, or request credentials. Users can disable or remove the plugin at any time. Questions can be reported through [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/arminazimi/evergreen/issues).

---

Source: https://arminazimi.github.io/evergreen/DETECTORS.html

# Detector authoring

Evergreen detectors are adapters at the detector SDK seam. They inspect a repository and return lifecycle findings; the scan engine handles detector attribution, sorting, reporting, and composition.

## Supported interface

Import the public SDK from `evergreen-deprecation/sdk`:

```ts
import {
  defineDetector,
  DETECTOR_API_VERSION,
  type Detector,
} from "evergreen-deprecation/sdk";
```

A compatible detector has one stable identifier and one operation:

```ts
export const detector = defineDetector({
  apiVersion: DETECTOR_API_VERSION,
  id: "example-ecosystem",
  async scan({ root }) {
    return [];
  },
}) satisfies Detector;
```

The interface guarantees:

- `root` is an absolute repository path.
- `id` uses lowercase letters, numbers, and single hyphens.
- `scan` returns findings without a `detector` field; the engine adds it from `id`.
- Findings must be deterministic for the same repository and bundled registry.
- Repository contents are untrusted input.
- The core contract provides no network capability. Detectors should use bundled, reviewed registry data so scans remain local and reproducible.
- An incompatible `apiVersion` fails before the detector scans.

See [`examples/detectors/todo-comments.ts`](../examples/detectors/todo-comments.ts) for a complete minimal adapter.

Built-in detectors with their own pages: [Container base images](detectors/container.md), [.NET](detectors/dotnet.md), [Go](detectors/go.md), [Java and Kotlin](detectors/java.md), [Kubernetes APIs](detectors/kubernetes.md), [Rust](detectors/rust.md), [Serverless runtimes](detectors/serverless.md), [Swift](detectors/swift.md). The C and C++, Ruby, PHP, Android, and CI runner images detectors have no separate pages yet; their supported declarations and limits are in [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#c-and-c-detector), [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#ruby-detector), [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#php-detector), [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#android-detector), and [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#ci-runner-images-detector).

## Ruby detector layout

The Ruby detector is a useful example of the layout a built-in detector follows. Its entry point, `src/detectors/ruby/index.ts`, finds the files, reads them, and matches each declaration to a rule. One pure parser per file type sits beside it (`parse-ruby-runtime.ts`, `parse-gemfile.ts`, `parse-gemfile-lock.ts`, and `parse-gemspec.ts`):

- A parser returns nothing, not an error, for a form it does not support, and never returns part of a malformed file or line.
- Rules come from `registry/ruby.json`, loaded through the bundled data. The detector takes a rule loader so tests can supply their own rules.
- A runtime pin uses the first rule whose `vers` range contains the version. A rule whose `vers` is malformed is skipped, so it does not hide a later rule.
- A `Gemfile` gem is matched only against rules that cover every version, while a `Gemfile.lock` gem is matched against any rule for that gem name.
- Gem rules that declare usage matchers use `analyzeSourceUsage`, so those findings list the Ruby files that import or call the gem. A `require`, `load`, `gem`, or `autoload` whose argument is not a string literal is unclassified. `require_relative` is never unclassified. Qualified calls without parentheses (for example `JSON.parse text`) are not matched.

The user-facing list of supported forms and limits for this detector is in [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#ruby-detector).

## PHP detector layout

The PHP detector follows the same layout. Its entry point, `src/detectors/php/index.ts`, finds the files, reads them, and matches each declaration to a rule. One pure parser per file type sits beside it (`parse-php-runtime.ts`, `parse-composer-json.ts`, and `parse-composer-lock.ts`):

- A parser returns nothing, not an error, for a form it does not support, and never returns part of a malformed file or line.
- Rules come from `registry/php.json`, loaded through the bundled data. The detector takes a rule loader so tests can supply their own rules.
- A runtime pin uses the first rule whose `vers` range contains the version. A constraint that is not a concrete version (for example `>=7.4` or `^8.2`) is skipped, and a rule whose `vers` is malformed is skipped, so neither hides a later rule.
- A `composer.json` package is matched only against rules that cover every version of the package, while a `composer.lock` package is matched against any rule whose `vers` contains the resolved version. An `abandoned` flag in the lockfile is recorded by the parser and is not itself a finding.
- Package rules that declare usage matchers use `analyzeSourceUsage`, so those findings list the `.php` files that `require` or `include` that package and the qualified calls those matchers name. A `require` or `include` whose argument is not a string literal is unclassified, as is `new $class` or `$class::method()`. Runtime end-of-life rules do not name source usages.

The user-facing list of supported forms and limits for this detector is in [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#php-detector).

## Android detector layout

The Android detector follows the same layout. Its entry point, `src/detectors/android/index.ts`, finds the files, reads them, and matches each declaration to a rule. Pure parsers sit beside it: `parse-build-gradle.ts` for SDK settings, `parse-settings-gradle.ts` for plugin pins, and `parse-libs-versions-toml.ts` for the version catalog. String-notation Maven dependencies in `build.gradle` and `build.gradle.kts` come from the Java detector's `parse-gradle.ts`; this detector keeps only those dependency declarations.

- A parser returns nothing, not an error, for a form it does not support, and never returns part of a malformed file.
- Rules come from `registry/android.json`, loaded through the bundled data. The detector takes a rule loader so tests can supply their own rules.
- A declaration uses the first rule whose `vers` range contains the version text. A rule whose `vers` is malformed, or whose comparison throws, is skipped, so it does not hide a later rule.
- An SDK setting matches `pkg:generic/android/<kind>` (`compileSdk`, `minSdk`, `targetSdk`, `buildToolsVersion`). An Android Gradle Plugin pin, in settings or the catalog `agp` key, matches `pkg:generic/android/agp`. `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` in settings matches `pkg:generic/android/kotlin-android`. The catalog `kotlin` key matches `pkg:generic/android/kotlin`. A string-notation dependency matches `pkg:maven/<group>/<artifact>`.
- Property references, method calls, version-catalog lookups, and `$` interpolation produce no declaration. The analysis reports no unclassified references.
- A rule that lists usage matchers uses `analyzeSourceUsage` for `.java` and `.kt` files. The bundled Play Billing rules do not list matchers, so those findings point at the declaration only.

The user-facing list of supported forms and limits for this detector is in [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#android-detector).

## CI runner images detector layout

The CI runner images detector follows the same layout. Its entry point, `src/detectors/ci-images/index.ts`, finds the files, reads them, and matches Azure hosted-image labels to a rule. One pure parser per file type sits beside it (`parse-gitlab-ci.ts`, `parse-circleci.ts`, and `parse-azure-pipelines.ts`):

- A parser returns nothing, not an error, for a form it does not support, and never returns part of a malformed file.
- Rules come from `registry/ci-images.json`, loaded through the bundled data. The detector takes a rule loader so tests can supply their own rules.
- An Azure `pool.vmImage` label of the form `ubuntu-<version>`, `macos-<version>`, or `windows-<version>` matches `pkg:generic/azure-pipelines/<family>-image` with an `intdot` version. Every rule whose `vers` range contains that version is reported. A label with an architecture suffix, or any other shape, is not matched.
- GitLab `image` and `services` values are always unclassified. CircleCI returns orbs, dynamic values, and floating aliases as unclassified; a literal CircleCI image is not matched, because this version has no CircleCI Package URL mapping.
- `latest`, `*-latest`, variables, and template expressions produce no finding. There is no source-usage pass.

The user-facing list of supported forms and limits for this detector is in [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#ci-runner-images-detector).

## Swift detector layout

The Swift detector follows the same layout. Its entry point, `src/detectors/swift/index.ts`, finds the files, reads them, and matches each declaration to a rule. One pure parser per file type sits beside it (`parse-swift-toolchain.ts`, `parse-package-swift.ts`, `parse-package-resolved.ts`, and `parse-xcode-project.ts`):

- A parser returns nothing, not an error, for a form it does not support, and never returns part of a malformed file or line.
- Rules come from `registry/swift.json`, loaded through the bundled data. The detector takes a rule loader so tests can supply their own rules.
- An exact pin (`.xcode-version`, `.swift-version`, `swift-tools-version`, `exact:` in `Package.swift`, a `Package.resolved` version, or an app-target `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET`) uses the first rule whose `vers` range contains the version. A rule whose `vers` is malformed is skipped, so it does not hide a later rule.
- A `from:` requirement in `Package.swift` is matched only against rules that cover every version of that package. Package identity is the lowercased repository name without `.git`, matching what SwiftPM writes in `Package.resolved`.
- The iOS deployment target is read only from application targets in `project.pbxproj` (`com.apple.product-type.application`), so a library or a `platforms:` minimum in `Package.swift` never produces that finding.
- Package rules that declare usage matchers use `analyzeSourceUsage`, so those findings list the `.swift` files that `import` that module and the qualified calls those matchers name. Runtime Objective-C lookup forms (`NSClassFromString`, `Selector(…)`, and similar) are unclassified. Toolchain and App Store rules do not name source usages.

The user-facing list of supported forms and limits for this detector is in [Swift](detectors/swift.md).

## C and C++ detector layout

The C and C++ detector follows the same layout. Its entry point, `src/detectors/cpp/index.ts`, finds the files, reads them, and matches each declaration to a rule. One pure parser per manifest sits beside it (`parse-cmakelists.ts`, `parse-conan.ts`, and `parse-vcpkg.ts`):

- A parser returns nothing, not an error, for a form it does not support, and never returns part of a malformed file.
- Rules come from `registry/cpp.json`, loaded through the bundled data. The detector takes a rule loader so tests can supply their own rules.
- A declaration with a version uses the first rule whose `vers` range contains that version. A rule whose `vers` is malformed, or whose comparison throws, is skipped, so it does not hide a later rule.
- A vcpkg dependency with no `version>=` matches only a rule that covers every version of that package. `cmake_minimum_required` matches `pkg:generic/cmake`. A Conan requirement matches `pkg:conan/<name>`. A vcpkg dependency matches `pkg:vcpkg/<name>`. Language standards, compiler checks, and `builtin-baseline` match the generic Package URLs named in the detector.
- Generator and module rules are not matched yet: the CMake parser does not emit those declarations. There is no source-usage pass.

The detector is experimental. Its five-repository public corpus includes a zero-finding case and independent ground-truth sources. The user-facing list of supported forms, lifecycle data sources, and limits is in [Compatibility](COMPATIBILITY.md#c-and-c-detector).

## Serverless runtimes detector layout

The Serverless runtimes detector follows the same layout. Its entry point, `src/detectors/serverless/index.ts`, finds the files, reads them, and matches each literal runtime identifier to a rule. One pure parser per file type sits beside it (`parse-template.ts`, `parse-serverless-yml.ts`, and `parse-tf.ts`):

- A parser returns nothing, not an error, for a form it does not support, and never returns part of a malformed file.
- Rules come from `registry/serverless.json`, loaded through the bundled data. The detector takes a rule loader so tests can supply their own rules.
- Each literal identifier is tried against `pkg:generic/aws-lambda-runtime/<id>` and `pkg:generic/google-cloud-functions-runtime/<id>`. The first rule whose VERS range contains the identifier wins. A rule whose VERS is malformed is skipped, so it does not hide a later rule.
- CloudFormation tags (`!Ref`, `!Sub`), Serverless `${…}` interpolations, Terraform `var` / `local` / interpolation values, and floating aliases such as `latest` produce no declaration.
- There is no source-usage pass: a runtime finding points at the declaration only.

The user-facing list of supported forms and limits for this detector is in [Serverless runtimes](detectors/serverless.md).

## Start a new detector in this repository

Do not copy an existing detector by hand. Generate the skeleton from a checkout of this repository:

```bash
npm ci
npm run build
node dist/src/cli.js new-detector go-modules --ecosystem go
```

The id is the detector's stable identifier (lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens, starting with a letter). `--ecosystem` is the registry slug and defaults to the id. The command creates nine files and nothing else:

| File | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `src/detectors/<id>.ts` | The detector. It imports only the public SDK, reports nothing yet, and says in its header what to do next. |
| `src/detectors/<id>/parse.ts` | A pure, bounded parser: contents in, `{ value, line }` declarations out. Its header lists the rules it keeps and a place to document the forms it deliberately does not read. |
| `registry/<id>.json` | An empty `evergreen.registry.v2` registry for your rules ([Lifecycle rules](RULES.md)). |
| `tests/<id>-detector.test.ts` | The conformance suite (determinism, zero-finding, malformed input) against the generated fixtures. |
| `tests/<id>-parse.test.ts` | The invariants every parser keeps: no throw on junk, bounded input and lines, determinism, 1-based lines. |
| `tests/fixtures/<id>/` | A README with a table of cases, and `zero/` and `malformed/` fixtures to replace with real ones. |
| `docs/detectors/<id>.md` | The page that describes what the detector reads, its rules, and its limits. |

The skeleton compiles and passes its own tests with zero rules, so every later change starts from a green build. The command refuses to run outside a checkout, refuses an id or ecosystem that an existing detector, registry file, or rule-id prefix already uses (it lists every clash and the file that holds it), and writes nothing if any target file exists.

After generating:

1. **Fixtures first.** Fill `tests/fixtures/<id>/` with small repositories: one positive per declaration type, lookalike negatives (comments, unrelated keys, dynamic values), a zero-finding one, and a malformed one. Describe each in the README table.
2. **Parser.** Teach `parse.ts` to read the declarations, one form at a time, each with a test. Bound the input, never evaluate what you read, and return nothing, not an error, for forms you do not support.
3. **Rules.** Add evidence-backed rules to `registry/<id>.json` ([evidence policy](../CONTRIBUTING.md#evidence-policy)).
4. **Detector.** In `<id>.ts`, find the files, parse them, and match declarations to rules. Report an exact path and line. Add the expected findings to the conformance test.
5. **Register it.** Add the detector to `builtInDetectors` in `src/detectors/index.ts`. To ship its rules in the signed data bundle ([Lifecycle data](DATA.md)), add the ecosystem to `BUNDLED_ECOSYSTEMS` in `src/data-bundle.ts`. The generator leaves both to you on purpose, so a skeleton never changes what scans report or what a data release contains.
6. **Check.** `npm run check` must pass, and `npm run validate:public-repos` must still match exactly. A new detector starts non-stable in `benchmarks/thresholds.json` until the corpus has meaningful coverage ([Validation](VALIDATION.md#precision-thresholds)).

Detectors that live outside this repository use the public SDK directly, as described below; `new-detector` is for contributors to Evergreen itself.

## Maturity

Every built-in detector has a level (`experimental`, `beta`, or `stable`) in `benchmarks/thresholds.json`. The level is what the detector promises users. [Decision 0013](decisions/0013-detector-maturity.md) defines those promises and the evidence that earns each level. The table below is that evidence, and `earnedLevel` in `benchmarks/thresholds.ts` checks the counts. A new detector starts as `experimental`.

A promotion is a pull request that changes `level` and records the corpus run the claim rests on: date, commit, precision, recall, and the counts below. For `beta` and `stable`, the thresholds file sets `stable` to `true`, so the corpus run enforces the precision floor. A demotion is the same pull request in reverse. It is also required when a full run shows precision or recall below the floor for that level and the gap is still open 30 days later.

### Promotion gates

A detector is named by the first segment of its rule ids. Conformance is the shared harness: determinism, locations, evidence, a mandatory zero-finding fixture, and malformed input that does not throw. "Repositories with findings" counts corpus repositories with at least one expected finding for that detector. "Zero-finding repositories" counts corpus repositories of the detector's ecosystem with no expected findings. A repository is blind when a rule fixed before the scan chose it. A repository picked because it contained a finding is targeted, and the corpus entry records `selection`. Every expected finding has a `groundTruthSource` that is independent of Evergreen's own output.

| Gate | Experimental → beta | Beta → stable |
